The handwritten copy used here, traced through other copies to the author's copy dated 1210 AH, calls it the Third Journey. That may fit better with the book's arrangement around the stages of the mystic's journey toward God. The editors worked hard to prepare and correct the text and to present it in a clear order. We thank God for enabling this work. We ask Him to help us publish the remaining volumes, and we thank the scholars who helped us print and correct this book. May God reward them. God is the giver of success and kindness. (Publisher)

Notes

  1. By “source” here, the author means the receptive source: the beginning of formation in the world of becoming, which comes with substantial motion and the natural renewal of things. In the case of the four elements, this means their ongoing change and their relation to pure receptivity—the first matter, which is pure potential and is drawn toward forms. The elements and natural forms move by their very nature. Since first matter is pure potential, it cannot by itself actively cause the soul or anything else to exist; if it could, it would no longer be pure potential. Nor can the elements, as bodies, be the active cause that brings something from nonexistence into existence. A giver must possess what it gives in a higher way than the recipient does. The cause must therefore be higher in existence than its effect. The elements are lower in existence than the soul, so they cannot be its active cause. The active cause of the soul and of all the perfections that come to first matter and its earliest forms is God’s pure providence, flowing down through every level.

    ↩

  2. The soul’s unity, which is identical with its existence, is a distinctive kind of unity: a comprehensive unity that gathers many levels of being. In one respect it is many within one; in another, one within many. In its own nature, the soul has a single, unified existence, including the forms that appear through it. Its branches and dependent powers are spread through it, as it were, by a process of descent. Taken in its full sense, the soul includes both this unified existence and its many branches. Its origin is one of its levels: prior to it in time, but later than it in essence. The levels that come earlier in time are one with those that come later in essence, though they differ in the direction of their development. So the soul is low in its height and high in its lowliness; it is pure even while embodied, and embodied even while immaterial. It is present in its branches without being inside them as one thing is inside another, and beyond them without being outside them as one thing is outside another. “Whoever knows himself knows his Lord.” Guard this insight from those who deny the mysteries of divine unity. The Imams have described it as a middle way between compulsion and complete freedom, between likeness and denial of likeness, and between negating God and comparing Him to created things.

    ↩

  3. “Possible” here means what can be brought into being by the Holy Emanation. Through the Most Holy Emanation, things are first measured out and given their timeless ordering. God’s providence is His knowledge of the best order before creation; that knowledge is active and brings what is known into existence. After His self-disclosure to Himself, God discloses Himself through His names and attributes and what follows from them, then through the individual things themselves. The first is His disclosure through the names and attributes, called the Most Holy Emanation; the second is His disclosure through the things that exist, called the Holy Emanation. The first is the mercy of His attributes, encompassing the intelligible meanings of things; the second is His active mercy, encompassing the existence of possible things.

    ↩

  4. If things were not brought into existence in this order, they would either all issue at once from the simple First Principle, which would mean that many things came from a source that is one in every respect, or they would issue in order with the least complete things first. The first option would make the First Principle composite; the second would make the lower things exist before the higher. Both are impossible. A cause must be most closely matched to its direct effect. If it were equally matched to several effects, there would be no reason for one rather than another to issue from it. The more complete thing is more closely matched to the cause than the less complete one. Also, the complete cause must contain in itself the full basis for its direct effect. If a lower effect came first and then caused the higher one, the First Cause would not fully account for the higher effect, and the cause would be less complete than its effect.

    ↩

  5. The reason is the one already given: if God’s providence stopped at a limit, His own being would be limited too. Far exalted is He above that.

    ↩

  6. “The first thing it received” follows from the earlier point that the outpouring cannot stop, or else the received thing would remain unchanged. The “rays” are an analogy for the giving of the generous First Principle through its intermediaries. The analogy is about how the effect spreads; the rays themselves are preparatory conditions, not active causes.

    ↩

  7. This gives an example of a sensible effect that even someone who relies only on the senses will recognize.

    ↩

  8. Matter is prepared for its kinds of perfection by its specific forms. Its specific perfections arise from those forms; its incidental readiness is an effect of its essential readiness. Matter is prepared by the forms it receives, not by itself, since as pure potential it is equally open to all perfections.

    ↩

  9. Strictly speaking, plants should not be called “living” in the sense of perceiving and acting: perception begins at least with touch, and action at least with movement by choice, neither of which plants have. It is true that existence itself is life flowing through all things, as the author insists elsewhere, though he criticizes Ibn Arabi for applying this idea to bodies in his discussion of the afterlife. But that broader sense does not fit this passage, where plants are distinguished from minerals and animals by the kind of life they have. Nor does it fit the phrase “the first thing matter receives,” which suggests that what came before plants lacked life in that sense.

    ↩

  10. A simple reality, such as necessary existence or existence in its absolute sense, has no source from which one could define it or prove it. One may still prove it through its effects or through the way it is affected, as one proves a reality from what it does. The same applies, even more clearly, to souls and forms. A form is another name for what makes a thing actual. A simple reality has no material or formal parts from which to define it or demonstrate it.

    ↩

  11. This follows the usual account. In the author’s own view, sensible things are perceived through the soul’s activity, and intelligible things through union with them and with the Active Intellect, as explained later.

  12. One could say that the soul, as soul, is material and exists in the body, as the author himself holds. His point is that calling it a “form” does not show that it has another level of existence, while “perfection” does not imply that it must inhere in something. A king completes a city, for example, without being a form impressed in it. The author is also reporting the philosophers’ preferred wording.

    ↩

  13. The soul’s perfection was just compared to a kind, and a kind is closer to a general category because it can be predicated of its instances. Form, by contrast, is compared with matter, which is farther from a general category: matter is considered on its own as something distinct, while a general category is predicated of things. The point is that something whose comparison is closer to the general category is a better candidate for the broader term in a definition. One could turn this argument around: form may be closer to meaning, or even be the same as the general category, while kind and matter differ only in how they are considered. These are arguments about what seems most fitting, not decisive proofs.

    ↩

  14. Matter is included in the idea of form because form points to the matter it informs. The idea of perfection, by contrast, points to the kind it completes, and a kind may be bodily or separate from matter. Thus defining the soul through perfection can include material souls such as plant souls and souls that are separate in their own nature.

    ↩

  15. This objection applies only if the definition is meant for animal soul alone and “power” means the power of movement. It does not apply if the definition is for soul in general, whether plant or animal, and “power” is understood broadly.

    ↩

  16. The issue is that a cause may be favored over another without any reason. One might reply that “power” means actuality in a broad sense and applies to all souls. The author’s point, however, is that definitions are about realities, not just words, and the soul in general has no existence apart from its particular instances.

    ↩

  17. “Perfection” can be used with the same meaning for both powers: it can mean the completion provided by the power of movement or the completion provided by both powers, as in the animal soul. “Power,” by contrast, is used in two different senses. If both are used in a definition, the word is equivocal; if one is chosen, there is no reason to prefer one over the other, and the definition leaves out part of the soul. It also fails to describe the soul as a whole, since the animal soul includes both powers. The point is that one and the same word, “perfection,” can apply to both without changing its meaning.

    ↩

  18. This objection has force. “Perfection” means that the soul completes a kind, as explained earlier. Although in reality the soul can also be called a perfection in another sense—because its two powers are one in being—this does not follow from the word itself.

    ↩

  19. “Limited” here may mean limited by one of the soul’s levels and by the body, or limited by the two together, or limited by the relation described in the definition.

    ↩

  20. The definition points to the soul and is measured by it; it does not mean that existence itself has definitions, as if definitions belonged to existence rather than to what a thing is.

    ↩

  21. The active cause here is the First Cause, God, and the active intellects. Things that depend on causes can be known only through their causes.

    ↩

  22. The question is what the soul is. People have held many views. Some, following Galen and his school, say that the soul is the body’s temperament or mixture. As long as the body keeps the temperament suitable to its kind, it is protected from corruption; once it loses that balance, the body dies. Others, including the theologian Imām al-Ḥaramayn, say that the soul is a fine, luminous body flowing through the body as water flows through a flower or fire through a coal. They say that this subtle body is addressed, rewarded, and punished, and that the visible body is kept together by it; when it leaves, the visible body quickly falls apart. Most Muʿtazilites and some Ashʿarites say that the soul is the visible body itself. Naẓẓām says it is an indivisible part located in the heart. In short, theologians have held nearly forty views, none supported by decisive proof. The most familiar is that the soul consists of original bodily parts that remain from the beginning to the end of life. It is astonishing that anyone who claims to follow reason would accept such accounts. The truth is what careful philosophers and mystics who have direct insight have taught: the soul is an immaterial substance that governs and preserves the body. Proofs will follow. A person can also test this by reflecting on the elements—earth, water, fire, and air—from which every bodily being is formed. Imagine the human being returned to those elements and set beside the elements outside the body. Could reason attribute the knowledge, wisdom, and power that make a fully developed human being God’s representative to earth, water, fire, air, or their mixture? No. Search within the earth and you will find a precious substance: a divine command and a sacred mystery. The author will later report the ancient philosophers’ views from Avicenna’s The Healing and interpret them.

    ↩

  23. The point is that it is false to say the soul’s true nature cannot be known from this definition. From the beginning, the soul is this relation to the body, and this relation is one level of its own being. The claim that it is a separate substance in its essence but related to the body only in its activity is wrong from the outset. If it existed before the body, that would be false; if it began to exist later, it would have no subject in which to begin, as will be explained.

    ↩

  24. A definition “by name alone” does not include a real nature. For example, the descriptions “black” and similar derived words do not correspond to one further thing in the world. “Black” refers to a body, which is a substance, and blackness, which is a quality; there is no third entity corresponding to the word. A definition of this kind does not include a distinct nature.

    ↩

  25. The exception is not quite of the same kind. The soul’s movement from bodily nature toward the Active Intellect is a strengthening of existence, one level after another. The soul that reaches the level of intellect preserves its earlier level as soul.

    ↩

  26. Most philosophers hold that the soul’s connection with the body follows from its coming into existence, rather than belonging to its nature. They also do not think it impossible for an immaterial and a material thing to form one kind. So neither premise in the two arguments is accepted by them. Both premises must be established for the arguments to work.

  27. One might object that the proof applies only if the soul’s nature necessarily requires a body, while the soul might be eternal or might have begun before the body. The author replies that the point is the conflict between saying the soul is a separate intellectual substance and saying it is connected to matter. There is also a problem if the soul is new: what subject could have received it? The argument does not depend on the word “then” meaning a later moment in time. In any case, the soul’s eternity has already been disproved. If someone says that a soul that comes into being must also perish, we answer that the soul’s bodily coming into being does not prevent its continued existence as a spirit.

  28. There are two kinds of relation. In one, the relation is part of what a thing is, or its nature is nothing but that relation; this is a category of relation. In the other, a thing’s nature belongs to another category, but its existence involves a relation. Matter, for example, is a substance by nature, though its existence involves a relation; blackness is a quality by nature, though its existence is entirely dependent on a subject. God has no created nature or category, yet descriptions such as creator and powerful apply to Him. The same distinction appears in things that flow or change. Motion and time are flowing by their very nature, while qualities, quantities, place, position, and natural forms may be stable in what they are but flowing in their existence. In one way or another, the physical world, with all its substances and accidents, is changing and passing away.

  29. The author uses this as a proof that existence is fundamental. If existence were only an idea drawn from things, blackness would be nothing but its particular nature. But blackness exists only as the existence of a subject; it is therefore a relation in its existence, even if it is a quality by nature.

  30. That is, separate from the body which the soul governs and completes.

  31. Earlier statements by the author point to this: the soul’s relation to the body follows from its relation of governing and acting on bodies; he also says that the soul is the body’s completion.

  32. A kind counts as an actual kind when it has the active source of these actions; it does not have to be carrying them all out. Having the power and source of the actions is enough.

We do not call someone “treating” while they only have the capacity to treat. There is a difference between being actually an animal or a geometer, and actually sensing, acting, or measuring.

The author later says that the soul is the first perfection of body considered without qualification; he means body without a restriction that would exclude its becoming a plant, animal, or human being. The soul is not a perfection of body taken as something complete and separate from all its forms. The author’s wording refers to both points.

  36. “Without any condition” means body as a general kind, not body considered as something already complete on its own.

  37. Material body means body taken as something complete and separate from whatever is joined to it. What is joined to this kind of body cannot be its first perfection.   38. “Natural body” can mean a body that is not a mathematical abstraction, a body that is not an imaginal or intermediate-world body, or a body that is not made by craft. The last meaning is intended here.

  39. The phrase “natural body” excludes forms such as the forms of a bed or other made objects. Even if one grants that a pilot’s soul completes a ship or a king’s soul completes a city, it is a perfection of an artificial body, not a natural one. If the entire ship or city together with the pilot or king were treated as one thing, that whole would not exist as one thing in the world. Existence and unity go together.

  40. “Tools” may be read as an adjective describing the natural body, or as a description of the soul, which acts through tools. Either reading is possible; the first is preferable. The phrase “not every natural body” qualifies “natural body,” not “perfection.”

  41. “Immaterial” is not being used here in its strict technical sense of “not existing in matter,” which would exclude plant and animal souls. It means that the soul is higher in its own level of existence than matter: its existence is not identical with the matter it informs.

  42. The intellect and soul, simply as intellect or soul, do not directly move the heavens. Yet the motion is still governed by the soul, because nature is subject to it.   43. The heavenly powers are distinct from the four elements, which are subject to coming-to-be and passing away.

  44. The theoretical and practical intellects in their potential or material stage.

    ↩

  45. There is no potential intellect in the heavens, since all the perfections of a heavenly body are already actual except for its positions.

  46. The intellect that forms part of the definition of “rational”—as in “a rational being is a soul with intellect”—does not mean a fully actual intellect.   47. These are images received from things that already have images. They affect an organ and the vital spirit, as when the two eyes or the vital spirit are affected at the meeting point of vision. They are like causal forms that precede what they cause, as God’s knowledge precedes what is known. There is no affected organ there, since the heavens have no eyes, ears, or anything like them. The forms flow to the heavenly spheres from within.

  48. This responds to Avicenna’s claim that this kind of perception does not occur in the heavens. Intellectual perception—the highest kind of knowledge through mental forms—is enough to call the heavens living, even if they do not sense or do not have forms impressed in them. If Avicenna means that sensation cannot occur there because no organ passively receives an image, the reply is the next argument. The author does not explicitly answer Avicenna’s claim that the heavenly intellect is actual while an animal’s is only potential. A better answer is that “living” means a being that can perceive and act; it does not require perception to be fully actual or passively received. One might ask why “power” can have two meanings here, when the soul’s definition was not allowed to use a word with two unrelated meanings. The reason is that “power” was equivocal between two categories: acting and being acted upon. These categories are different kinds of possible things, with no shared essence. Perception, by contrast, is grounded in existence. Knowledge, life, will, and power follow existence and are identical with it in their reality, each according to its own level. Perception is therefore one shared idea, even though one kind of perception is active and another receptive.

  49. The author’s point is that the concept of a body’s being able to act does not rule out its being preceded by another state.   50. “A ship’s being useful” means its being in a condition where it can perform its function. The concept does not exclude the possibility that an earlier condition was needed; it does not mean that such a condition must have been needed.

  51. That is not the point. The author means that the soul and the body’s ability to perform the actions of life are not one thing. As the ship’s usefulness may be preceded in time, the body’s ability to perform the actions of life is preceded by the soul. The body’s ability to burn and the heat in it, by contrast, are the same thing: its ability to burn is simply its having heat.

  52. Avicenna says in The Healing that a body’s being able to perform an action or have a quality can happen in two ways. In the first, some other thing in the body produces that action or quality. In the second, nothing other than that state exists in the body: for someone who identifies heat with the body’s being able to burn, the heat in the body is exactly that capacity. At first glance, the soul might seem to be like heat in this second sense, but that cannot be right. The soul is not the same as a body’s being able to produce the acts of life.

  53. “Rather” marks a stronger claim: we establish that life must be preceded by another condition, not merely that it might be.

    ↩

  54. The author is not repeating his earlier point that life itself is the soul, where life was defined as a body’s ability to carry out the actions of life.   55. “Second” means second in the order of the discussion, not second in rank.

  56. This is the second kind of case: something that is not a body may have an existence that is the same as its being alive. This applies to most nonbodily beings, including the First Being, the intellects, and souls.

  57. The issue is not whether this part exists in something that is not a subject. Simply existing in something other than a subject does not make a thing a substance; blackness, for instance, exists in a body, and the body itself does not exist in a subject. The clue is the author’s reply that something may be a part of a whole.

    ↩

  58. For example, blackness exists in a compound whose nature depends on that part. The unstated premise is that anything inhering in a subject depends on that subject.

    ↩

  59. “Essential” and “accidental” are relative terms. Animal is essential to human being but accidental to “rational,” which is a distinguishing feature of animal. In the same way, the general kind is a general feature in relation to the distinguishing feature, while the distinguishing feature is a specific feature in relation to the general kind.

    ↩

  60. Not every substantial feature is a substance—color, for example, is substantial to blackness—and not every accidental feature is an accident in the technical sense. “Human” is accidental to “rational,” but is neither identical with it nor one of its parts.

    ↩

  61. The answer follows from the earlier point that a part can exist within a whole without being in a subject, as blackness exists in the whole made up of blackness and its subject. If something is not an accident in relation to a particular thing, it need not be a substance in relation to it; it may be neither. Zayd, for example, is neither one nor many in the sky, though he is one in himself and in the place he occupies.

    ↩

  62. “Accident” in the classification of kinds—such as general or specific accident, essential or nonessential feature—means a feature that can be predicated of something, such as “walking” or “laughing.” “Accident” in the ten categories means something that exists in a subject that does not depend on it, such as walking or laughter. The soul might exist in a subject and so be an accident in this technical sense, while also being a part of a compound, as already explained. Or the souls in question may be different in nature; perhaps the reference is to plant souls and animal souls that are impressed in matter.

    ↩

  63. The “feature” here is like what logicians call a describing predicate. It may be identical with its subject, be part of it, or be something outside it. It does not mean an accidental quality that exists in something else. Life is essential to body because both exist through one and the same existence; being alive does not require adding another feature to an already complete body, as a white body requires adding whiteness. Here “body” means body considered together with life—in other words, animal. “Completes” means that it makes the thing actual. The proof is this: we observe life’s effects in animals. They cannot come from bodyhood shared by all bodies, or every body would produce them. They cannot come from first matter, which is purely receptive and cannot act. Life must therefore be essential to the body in the sense of body that includes life. Its source is a form that completes the matter from which the general kind is made. A form that completes matter is a substance, so the soul is a substance. The argument depends on life being essential to the animal body; if life were accidental, its source would also be an accident, as blackness is the source of being black. Some people thought life was accidental because they saw that bodies decay, and failed to distinguish body considered as complete and separate from further forms from body considered as open to them. The latter is alive in itself. An animal is a kind of body, and “rational” is true of some bodies as well; predication means that the subject and predicate are one in existence. The view that every body is lifeless also conflicts with the principle that a simple thing contains the perfections of what lies beneath it. The author’s account is consistent with substantial motion: all the stages from beginning to end are one continuous existence. This may also help answer those who accept only the spiritual afterlife, provided they still affirm a body—though the author considers that view incomplete. The body required for the afterlife is a formed body, and the afterlife is a realm of living beings.

    ↩

  64. A universal considered with “universality” added to it is only an idea; it does not exist in the world. “A hidden individual” here does not mean that a universal may exist as a universal. It means that the term “universal” can be applied to something that is not itself qualified by universality, or to an individual that falls under it.

    ↩

  65. The proof establishes that the soul is a substance in the sense that it completes a substantial kind—just as first matter, bodily form, and specific forms are called substances in that sense. It does not show that the soul itself belongs to the category of substance as a fully defined kind. A substantial form and the distinguishing features drawn from it are not themselves kinds within the category of substance; they are called substances because they complete a substantial kind.

    ↩

  66. The apparent circle is resolved by saying that the soul’s coming into being depends on temperament, while the temperament’s continued existence depends on the soul.

  67. The author’s considered view is that the elements do not retain their pure forms. This is clear if substantial forms can grow stronger or weaker and change while preserving something of their original nature.

  68. The first possibility—matter made of several elements—refers to the view that elemental forms remain. The second—simple matter—refers to the view that they do not.

  69. The question is whether the celestial sphere could force the elements to stay together. In that case, their mixture would result from a period of interaction under force.   83. The comparison with fire suits the author’s account of the soul as having levels, beginning with natural power and ending, as God wills, at the highest level. I say that the commentator’s phrase “one unfolding process” points to substantial motion: the earlier and later stages are not separate things, one merely deficient and the other complete, but are like dim and bright light. The author’s denial of substantial motion should be understood as affirming that the divine aspect within every thing is stable. His use of “substance” for a thing’s inner reality is not unusual.   84. A careful reader will see that the passage quoted from Naṣīr al-Dīn al-Tusi plainly affirms that substance grows stronger. It cannot be read in any of the three ways the author lists.

  85. The second option means that the earlier forms remain but hand over the work of governing to a later form, then become inactive. The third means that the earlier form is destroyed and another form comes into being to act for itself. There is also a fourth possibility: the earlier form remains when the later one arrives, does not hand over its actions, and each effect comes from the source suited to it. Until this option too is ruled out, the conclusion does not follow that all these effects come from one source with different levels of strength. The commentator leaves it aside because it is clearly false. If forms develop by degrees from complete to more complete, each later form must do what the earlier one could do, and more. This also follows from the principles that one matter must have one form, one kind one distinguishing feature, and one effect one cause.

    ↩

  86. In the first option, the power is said to destroy its matter; in the second, it is said to make the matter ready for something that will destroy it. “Or” here introduces a stronger correction: the power prepares its own matter to receive what destroys the power itself. One might object that the questioner did not say what destroys the earlier form; perhaps outside events do so, as one material form replaces another. The answer is that we are discussing natural development and completion, not destruction by outside or inside causes. A form in matter exists to constitute and complete that matter, and in a compound to preserve its mixture and structure. It cannot exist to destroy the matter or prepare it to receive what will destroy the form. Avicenna distinguishes two kinds of change. In one, the earlier thing naturally moves toward a more complete state: a child becoming an adult does not lose a substantial part of its nature, but completes it. In the other, the earlier thing’s nature does not tend toward the later one, as when water becomes air. In that case, the first nature does not remain in the second; it is destroyed. Here, the stages of one soul are like the first kind, not the second. If each stage were created and destroyed in an instant, there would be infinitely many separate acts of coming-to-be and passing away between fixed endpoints, and instants would follow one another without any duration. The same issue arises whenever one soul seems to change into another, as from plant to animal, or between different levels within plant or animal life. Nature does not leap over stages. Nor is this a case of forced change: when a plant is cut or an animal burned or drowned, the nearby matter is destroyed. In natural development, the same matter remains. If all upward development were forced, it would have to be forced either always or in most cases, which is impossible. So the mover that restores the body to health is not its temperament. It is like the natural power that restores an ordinary state after an unnatural, forced one has been removed; it is neither of the two states themselves.

  93. Strictly speaking, there are no separate parts here: the sphere is one continuous whole, and continuity goes with its being one individual. But elemental forms remain in generated bodies, so their parts are not truly continuous; the elements’ particles are small and touch one another. The argument therefore concerns the nearby matter, such as nerve or bone, which is one whole. If it concerned more distant matter, different parts of the matter could have different shapes.

  107. The soul would be an incomplete cause of the whole. As part of the whole, it would be a substance; because the body exists without it in the general sense of body, it would be an accident in relation to that subject.

  108. Their reason is the circularity they will now describe: an accident depends on its subject, so if the subject also depended on the accident, each would depend on the other.   109. The second view is false for the reasons already given about substances and accidents. A state depends on its subject to be an individual, but the subject need not depend on that state in the same way. The subject may depend on it for its existence as a body, or for its specific kind; neither relation makes the dependence circular. An accident, by contrast, depends on a subject that is independent of it in both existence and kind. The first view is also false: if the compound forms a genuine unity, one existence cannot be both a substance and an accident. If it does not form a genuine unity, then the soul is not truly a part of it, as a stone placed beside a person is not part of that person.

  110. A feature belongs essentially to a thing only when the thing is understood in its full nature, not when it is merely described by something true of it in a general way. A definition, for example, gives the full nature, while an incomplete description gives only part of it.

At death, something like the fire’s heat remains in a wall after sunset.   117. A general kind taken without further qualification produces an effect only when joined to a distinguishing feature. Philosophers sometimes attribute a general effect to a general cause, but without such a feature the general kind has no independent existence and cannot produce an effect. This is why the source of the effect is the distinguishing feature. One may object that we can imagine “animal” without adding a distinguishing feature. The reply is that this imagined “animal” is a kind of mental matter, not the general kind as it exists in a real thing. What is vague in existence is not the same as what is vague in thought.

  118. The point is that if the plant power were not a service of the animal power, it would have to operate through an artificial arrangement of parts, which is false. In the author’s account of substantial motion, the power of nourishment, growth, and reproduction is an early level or sign of the animal or human soul, the enduring source from which the powers arise. At the beginning, its only actions are nourishment and related functions.

  119. A simple reality contains all the perfections of the things below it in a higher, more unified way. The soul sees the detailed powers within its unity, and the powers reveal the soul’s unity within their detail. The cause contains a complete account of its effect; the effect contains only an incomplete account of its cause. So the soul is its powers, and its powers are the soul.

  120. “Perceptive actions” are clear. “Animal actions” are those of desire and anger. “Plant actions” include digestion, nourishment, and growth. “Natural actions” include preserving the temperament, shaping the matter, and joining its parts.

  121. The soul’s different kinds make things different in their essential nature.   122. The word “powers” is often used for actual powers and active sources, as when Aristotle calls God the “divine power.” It may also be used because, relative to the earthly soul, the soul is a general kind with two kinds beneath it: heavenly and earthly. Each of these can be divided further: animal souls include the souls of horses, donkeys, and other animals, and plant souls are divided in the same way. Inwardly, the human soul too is a general kind with distinct kinds beneath it; outwardly, it is the final, indivisible species, because its definition is one. Avicenna may be using “kinds” in its technical sense, or simply to mean classes in the ordinary sense.

  124. The powers branching from the soul, and the organs assigned to them, are described here as earlier philosophers described them. This differs from what anatomists and biologists say today.   125. Read “then” rather than “and,” and read the verb in the passive. The shaping and actual likeness occur in the womb. The reproductive power prepares each part of the material to receive its own particular form, as explained earlier.

  126. The motive power is what sets desire for an end in motion. There are several ways to understand Avicenna’s claim that it is the final cause. First, in reality it may be identical with the final cause: the end is what desire seeks, and the seeker and what is sought belong to one kind. Light seeks light, fire seeks fire, and good things seek what is good for them. This is why one says that love begins in the substantial likeness between lover and beloved. In truth, seeker and sought are one; lover and beloved come from one source, as in the saying: “I am the one I love, and the one I love is me.” Second, the motive power may be identical with the final cause in thought. The end comes first in thought but last in the action itself. Voluntary actions are preceded by imagining and judging the end. The imagined end is the object perceived, and the perceiving power is also the power that moves, since all the powers are aspects of one soul. Though Avicenna did not affirm the union of knower and known except in The Origin and Return, he allows a meaningful connection between the powers and between the powers and what they perceive. Third, the claim may mean that the motive power’s own fulfillment, as it achieves what it desires, is the true final cause of the soul’s actions—not merely the apparent ends of particular crafts, such as a king sitting on a throne as the carpenter’s goal, or Zayd taking shelter in a house as the builder’s goal.

There are therefore three perceiving powers, because a relation and its object must match in number: common sense perceives images, and imagination stores them; estimation perceives particular meanings, and memory stores them; intellect perceives universal meanings, and the Active Intellect is their storehouse. The power that works with them all is the one that combines and separates.

So the second example, which distinguishes actions by their presence or absence, also makes sense. The author lists possible reasons for different sources and powers in general, then asks which ones account specifically for the different powers of the soul. The premise is obvious and agreed on; the disagreement is whether such an object exists. The theologians say that everything, even the Necessary Being, has several aspects. Nothing is one in every respect, they say, since then it could produce only one thing.

  144. There are several problems with this argument. First, the author himself applies the principle to nature, following the philosophers: one nature in one recipient produces one effect, such as a sphere. Second, in the discussion of divine matters he expressly states the principle: what is purely one, and anything considered simply as one, produces only one effect through that aspect. Third, although something that is not purely one may have several aspects, not every aspect suits every effect. One nature might produce a polygon because its general aspect gives the surface and its distinctive aspect gives the lines. Otherwise, why could fire not produce both light and darkness, or nature both motion and rest, with no condition such as being in or out of the natural place?

  145. The philosophers did reply that color itself is what sight perceives directly, while the particular shade is perceived incidentally and as a secondary object of attention.   146. In fact, both proofs apply, and there is also a third kind mentioned earlier: concepts may differ because they oppose one another, as two actions can contradict each other.

  147. This is not the earlier, rejected argument from an action’s being present or absent. That argument concerned the actions themselves; this one concerns the powers that produce them. This kind of evidence is what careful investigators rely on for all powers. In natural powers, the examples are as already given. In inner perception, imagination may be impaired while memory and rational thought remain sound. For example, a patient with a disturbance of imagination may think that people are in his house playing music without pause and ask his family to remove them, yet still recognize friends and enemies because his memory is sound. A different patient may have a disorder of thought while imagination and memory remain intact: he locks himself in a room, opens a window, and asks passers-by whether they would like him to throw something to them. When they name an object, he throws it to them. Unlike the first patient, he does not imagine anything; his memory tells him what he is throwing and what it is for, but his impaired reasoning does not let him see that his action is mistaken. A disturbance in the rear of the brain may impair memory while leaving the other powers intact. At the beginning of an illness, the defect can be isolated in one power. As it worsens, it may spread to neighboring powers because their locations are close, and then the powers can no longer be distinguished in this way.

  148. Do not think that growth continues in hair and nails, and that this rescues the claim that the power of growth never fails. Growth means a proportional increase in the three dimensions of the body’s original parts. Hair and the like are surplus material driven out by smoky vapour. There is another reason why an essential feature may cease to appear.

  149. We can say that one power is absent while another remains only by knowing that the effect of one has ceased while the effect of the other continues. If different effects always required different powers, the author’s first argument would succeed. Keep this point in mind.

  150. One might object that this reasoning also undermines the author’s view. If one cause can have several aspects and produce many effects, why could one power not produce an effect when a condition is present and cease when it is absent? Similarly, opposite effects might follow from two opposing conditions, as heat softens wax while the nature of salt makes it hard. One might also cite matter and form: the author says they are united, yet they can be separated.

    We answer that if the conditions are merely explanatory or qualifying aspects in thought, they cannot account for genuinely opposite effects, since they do not make the subject itself multiple. If they are real, joined aspects, then this is precisely what we mean by several powers. One could say that the soul grows when considered under its growth aspect and nourishes when considered under its nutritive aspect. If you agree that there are distinct powers, there is no dispute about what to call them: call them powers, conditions, or real aspects. This differs from the merely conceptual aspects assigned to the First Intellect, which do not make its sources of action multiple. Its effects do not come from one cause in the same way: some issue from it directly, others incidentally. As for matter and form, the real separation is between an imaginal form and matter; they were never united in the first place.

This proposal mirrors the earlier claim that one soul has several powers; it is no more decisive than that claim.

  152. Some copies read “not needed.” Both readings make sense: reproduction is needed for preserving the species, but not for preserving the individual.

  154. The commentator is saying that the claim that the soul knows particulars through instruments is also held by the philosophers. On their account, the soul perceives universals in itself, while particulars are perceived by its instruments; the instruments perceive them, and the soul has no direct awareness of them. The commentator thinks the author’s words show that he mistakenly attributes this view to earlier philosophers, and that he himself held it for much of his life before changing his mind. But “perceiving particulars through instruments” does not mean that the soul is unaware of them. On the earlier philosophers’ account, particular images are impressed in the instruments, and the soul is directly aware of the instruments and their contents. It does not receive an image reflected from the instrument, nor is the image of a particular impressed in an immaterial power. On the author’s account, the images subsist in the powers that receive them, but that existence is an expression of the soul’s own existence, since those powers are its essential aspects.

  155. That is, the perceiver is present to itself. Perception is presence, which is why the author can say that the soul perceives through a given thing. Affirming something requires first conceiving both sides of the claim.

The organ may be called “healthy” in a relative sense. Another possibility is that it cannot be affected by the power—that is, by the directly perceived forms. Since these powers are bodily, their instruments must be affected by their action, at least as a preparation for perception, as the author holds.

The point is not that matter is itself perceived—matter is not present to a perceiving power. Rather, when the sense power is present and a similar quality reaches it, perception follows, as it does in other comparable cases. These qualities prepare the organ for perception. This is the more likely reading.

  159. The organs can receive a power that exists in them once they are fully prepared for it. They can therefore receive what that power perceives, since a recipient must be suited to what it receives, just as the perceiver must be suited to what it perceives.

  160. “Conditions” and “impediments” are used in their ordinary sense of defining features, as when we say that a human being, on the condition of being able to speak, has this nature, or that a donkey, on the condition of braying, has that nature.

  161. From the perspective of divine metaphysics, all possible existence—the realm of action—is a shadow of the divine realm of unity. That realm in turn follows from the divine attributes, gathered in the simple unity of the divine essence. If the complete order of possible existence, in its downward or upward levels and in its length and breadth, were deficient, existence itself would be deficient. Consider this carefully.

  162. In their terminology, the instruments of perception include the nerves and vital spirit, especially in the language of natural philosophers. That is likely what the author means by “powers in the sensory instruments.” Sometimes “instrument” also means a power considered as an instrument of the soul, as in the definition of the soul as the first perfection of an instrumental body. If “instrument” means a bodily organ, the author’s point is clear. If it means a power, he is denying that the image inheres in the power as a quality, as is commonly supposed. When he says that perception is not the organ’s reaction to an external thing, he is also denying that perception is an effect of the material object itself. The organ’s reaction, together with its position relative to matter bearing a quality, prepares the soul to produce within its own world an image that resembles that quality. On the author’s view, sensation is therefore an active process. The claim he rejects—that perception consists in an image being present in an instrument—is not the same as his claim that the image exists in the perceiver itself. If the instrument means a power, what he rejects is the image’s inherence in that power; what he affirms is that it exists through the power as an expression of the soul.

  163. This supports the earlier point that the recipient must be considered together with the quality actually present in it. The argument here sums up what was just explained.

  164. One might object that this concedes the point: different defining features produce different effects, and sharing a general kind does not help. The author’s point is that the animal’s nutritive power shares something real with the plant’s nutritive power, and also includes sensation and voluntary movement. If the shared “nutritive power” were only a word used in two unrelated ways, or a concept common to two beings that differ completely in their real natures, then the powers of nourishment and sensation would be one and the same. Nourishment would come from the sensitive power, and sensation and movement from the nutritive power, because the general nature would itself differ rather than being specified by distinct features. That is like color, whose general existence is one with the distinctive features that separate its kinds.

    But if the shared kind is a real general nature specified in different ways—as with compound bodies, which can be considered as substance, as having dimensions, as body, as growing body, or as sensing body—then the question remains whether the general nature and its distinguishing feature are one existence or several. If sensation and voluntary movement came from the shared, fully formed general nature, plants would also sense and move by choice. Otherwise, the existence of distinct powers is established. This is the philosophers’ view; the author’s own account will be given later, when he defines nourishment and growth and treats powers as simple. The philosophers also hold that effects differing in kind come from different sources. Since the actions of nutritive powers share a kind, they come from a nutritive power of that kind; sensation and voluntary movement differ in kind from nourishment and therefore come from another source. In that sense, their use of “nutritive power” for distinct beings is only verbal: there is no common meaning between powers whose whole natures differ.

In the latter, the image exists in the knower, not in matter. The two kinds of image differ in eight ways, discussed earlier in the section on intellect and intelligible things.

  171. In truth, the soul, insofar as it produces natural actions, is not aware of itself or of those actions. Nature is plainly not aware of itself or of its effects.

  172. The author has granted that knowledge of the cause exists, but that knowledge of the effect does not. More precisely, knowledge of the cause does not exist at the soul’s low level in this instance. The soul acts naturally in producing its bodily effects, just as natural powers do. Yet in relation to those powers, which are its own aspects, the soul acts through self-disclosure; its awareness of them is direct and unified. Its knowledge of the powers as they exist at their own levels is like God’s complete, unified knowledge of things through their own existence. The powers here are like the things there: they are relations whose existence depends entirely on the knower.

  173. The First Intellect does not exist at the same level as the lower things of which it is said to be ignorant. If those things’ existence is their knowledge, then the First Intellect’s lack of their existence is its ignorance of them. Yet the First Intellect’s existence is nobler than theirs. Consider this carefully.

  174. This “ignorance” is the absence, in the First Intellect, of a lower level interwoven with nonexistence. The First Intellect contains that level in a higher way, but its own intellectual level is precisely the absence of the lower level. That absence is ignorance; this ignorance is the source of all beings and is nobler than knowledge of those lower things. The philosopher’s words may also mean that the First Intellect is unaware of everything below God because it is absorbed in witnessing divine beauty and majesty. There is a report that God has creatures who do not know that He created Adam or Iblīs. A reading closer to the view held by Aristotle’s followers is this: natural things, considered as material, do not exist as knowledge for the intellect, because they exist in matter, remain hidden by spatial distance and temporal extension, and are not present as unified forms. Knowledge depends on formal existence and presence. They are known through images that exist in the intellect, but in a way that expresses the intellect rather than inhering in it. They may also be said to be known directly in another sense: knowledge is a form present to the knower, and this is true of the thing represented as well as of the image; the image is a tool for attending to the thing, not the thing attended to in itself.

    ↩

  175. That is, inward insight: the vision of an intellect illuminated by inner awareness, gained through spiritual discipline and exercises that keep the soul turned towards the source of knowledge and its light.

    ↩

  176. This does not apply to attraction. The body does not seek it by nature; it is harmful to the patient, and the body resists it.

    ↩

  177. Recall what we said near the beginning of the First Journey about definitions and proofs. The author’s definition of nourishment—and likewise his definition of growth—is a complete demonstration: it gives the full proof. If he had said only “the nutritive power replaces what is lost,” that would be a definition that serves as the starting point of a proof. If he had said only “it changes food so that it resembles the substance being nourished,” that would give the result of the proof.

    ↩

  178. Maybūdī says that the power should be called “the growth-giving power,” but the philosophers used a name that parallels “nutritive power.” I say that this wording hints at what the author has established: the body is a level of the soul. They describe the power through a bodily feature to point to a kind of unity between body and soul. We can infer the same unity from their calling power “a quality of the soul,” even though it is a quality that exists in the force spread through the muscles. Unless that force were a level of the soul, it would not have a quality of the soul. Hold to this point.

    ↩

  179. That is, after the age when growth stops, from then until the end of life. The author mentions this case because it makes the difference clearer. Fatness before that age is not growth either; nor is thinness during that age the same as decline.

  180. This refers to the kind of cause called aṭrūqiyā.

    ↩

  181. In reality, there are two powers here. The wording suggests this by introducing them with “as for,” even though the author has not yet stated that two powers preserve the species. The reproductive power clearly does so. The formative power’s role is less clear, since the body needs the forms of bones, veins, nerves, and flesh, and its individual matter does not need these forms in the same way it needs reproductive moisture to preserve the individual. The answer is that “forms” here means the shapes and patterns that distinguish individuals as members of their kinds. Without the formative power’s work, the kinds would not remain distinct. The test for a cause is whether its absence would entail the absence of its effect. Without reproduction, the species would not continue; without formation and its patterns, the species would not continue as distinct kinds. This does not mean that the individual would immediately cease to exist, since the nutritive power replaces what the body loses. But saying that this individual would no longer remain an individual of its kind amounts to saying that the kind itself would not remain.

  182. Unlike yellow bile and black bile, phlegm has no single organ of its own. It is spread through the other organs because of their moisture and helps keep them from drying out. When the body lacks food, phlegm may be transformed into blood—unless the point is that some of it flows to the brain, and likewise the lungs, to nourish them.

    ↩

  183. One might say that all this proves only that the fluids are distinguished, not that the nutritive power does the distinguishing; perhaps a separate distinguishing power does that. We reply that attraction already accounts for the distinction: the spleen attracts black bile and the gall bladder attracts yellow bile, for example. A separate power would do no further work and would be an unnecessary, idle addition. Attraction is needed in every organ, while a distinct sorting power is not. Also, the fluids are not entirely separated: a little yellow bile remains in blood to thin it and help it pass through narrow vessels, and a little black bile remains to give it a consistent texture.

  184. This qualification excludes some forms of jaundice caused by a blockage in the bile duct.

  185. The point is that “end” can mean either the point a movement reaches or the purpose for which it is undertaken. Since these are different, they require different powers, just as an animal has an active power and a power of desire. The active power always has an endpoint, even in a pointless or random action: like nature, it brings movement to a particular limit. It carries out its assigned task, but it is not what supplies the purpose. For example, a stone thrown at Zayd’s head reaches and wounds him; the hand’s active power strikes a hated person. But the purpose—relieving the thrower’s anger or making Zayd submit—is the work of desire. These are two different ends and require two sources. The same applies to the plant powers: digestion moves food to the point where its blood form ends, while nourishment acts for the sake of the organ’s form.

    ↩

  186. Pure matter has no feature that would make it ready for one form rather than another. If the first matter of wheat and barley were exactly the same, there would be no reason for one to become wheat and the other barley. Their elements are the same, but each stage is prepared by the form that came before it: an earlier wheat form prepares matter for the next wheat form, and an earlier barley form prepares it for the next barley form. The same question can be asked about those earlier forms, and so on. The philosophers allow—and indeed require—this succession, so that the flow of existence does not stop. The same applies to a sequence of forms in one matter, as in semen: each new stage, such as a clot or a small lump of flesh, changes what the matter is ready to receive.

  187. The objector would not accept that the inference from “matter alone is not enough” is valid, because he recognizes no agent other than God and considers the matter’s reactions sufficient for the outpouring. The commentator therefore adds the principle that every reaction and readiness in matter depends on an agent’s action.

  188. One argument is specific to the stomach and intestines; the other applies to all the organs.

    ↩

  189. The difference is that one power may be weak where another is strong, and vice versa. It is not that one of the powers is completely absent.

  190. The food drawn from outside into the stomach is not what nourishes the stomach. The blood drawn from the liver through vessels in the stomach wall nourishes it; the text itself points to this when it mentions what the stomach draws from the liver. The three actions mentioned next concern nourishment of the whole body; the later three concern blood drawn from the liver to nourish the stomach itself. Some copies read “the powers that retain in the substance of the stomach,” which is the better reading.

  191. The commentator means that some writers loosely call this a doubling. More accurately, there are four powers that produce food and four preparatory powers that resemble them.

  192. The four powers that produce nourishment are clear. The four preparatory powers that help digestion and expulsion throughout the body may be understood as follows. Digestion strengthens the qualities of fluids in the stomach. The spleen releases some black bile at the entrance to the stomach, which irritates and contracts it and thereby arouses hunger. The gall bladder releases some yellow bile into the intestine; its irritating quality prompts the bowel to expel its contents. Expulsion also occurs in the testes.

    ↩

  193. Some copies say “not resembling it.” This may refer to the condition of people with leprosy or vitiligo. Consider the wording carefully.

    ↩

  194. One might object that plants feed on a simple body, namely water. The answer is that water does not become food for a plant until it mixes with earth.

  195. This is like air around an overturned bowl placed over a fire: when its form is disrupted, the air is prepared to receive the form of water from the giver of forms. In the same way, suitable moist bodies next to the living body prepare its matter to receive the actual form of nourishment from the soul, continuously and through renewed instances. The same idea applies to the body’s light or color: it comes from the soul’s emanations and levels. What the soul preserves is not simply the same material body that remains after death, but a different matter and temperament; the soul is not the immediate cause of the color and shape left behind.

    The nature that brings fatigue is also not the same as the nature that serves the soul. The bodily matter, nature, and powers are levels of the soul when considered without restriction, and are linked to it spiritually. Something even more surprising has been said in divine metaphysics: the air that carries speech, or the tablet on which a speaker writes, is not a separate object in the ordinary sense. Considered as the medium of the speaker’s act, the speech exists through the speaker.

    The soul is a complete expression of divine unity and bears all the names of God. It has natural qualities as well as the qualities of spiritual beings, potentially or in actuality. So it contains natural powers and bodily aspects in its own right. Just as a higher thing contains the perfections of what is lower in a higher way, the lower effects that flow from it do not make the higher thing lose its level; they are its appearance and expression at lower levels. Some souls possess knowledge and perfection from within themselves, without needing the preparation of hearing or sight. Others acquire them after preparation, but even then the perfection comes from within the soul, not from foreign material things.

    The same applies to nourishment. In the senses and intellect, the soul is completed by forms that are present to it directly, not by external things known only indirectly. Its bodily nourishment at the level of nature and body likewise comes from the soul. So the “food from the world of the soul” is not food that is merely potential, even if only nearly ready to nourish: it is food in actuality. And actual food here means its form, not its matter. The author speaks as though food were the matter because, in his view, matter and form are united and matter is absorbed into form. “The world of the soul” means its lower, formal level. This should not seem too strange: the original forms of the organs come from the soul, since the formative power is a lower level of the soul; the replacement of what those organs lose comes from the soul as well. The soul brings together the worlds of meaning and form. It is like clear air touched by a cold wind: clouds appear without vapour rising from below, yet the air does not leave its own higher state.

    Forgive this long explanation. This is a difficult point and a common source of doubt and missteps.

    ↩

  196. At every moment, the body that is nourished is made up of different parts from the body at the previous moment. The whole would cease to exist whenever any part disappeared. That is not so if the stages of its form appear through one enduring, individual soul, which remains the source of all the stages. This applies the principle already mentioned: every natural or psychic substance is one thing in actuality. Keep this point in mind.

    ↩

  197. The perceiver must be one with what it perceives; otherwise it would not be completed by it or move from potentiality to actuality. This is the major premise of an unstated argument: the sense is completed by what it senses, and whatever is completed by something is identical with it. Therefore the sense is identical with what it senses.

  198. Just as the intellect has four stages, from intellect in potentiality to intellect in actuality, digestion also has four stages, from food in potentiality to food in actuality. The note may instead compare the four degrees of abstraction in knowledge: perception by the senses abstracts from matter while requiring the presence of matter; imagination does not require matter, though its images retain shape, size, and similar features; estimation is more abstract, though its objects remain tied to measurable things; and intellect is fully abstract and free of matter. The four stages of cleansing and digesting food follow the same pattern. The author’s phrase “understanding” in place of “knowledge” is not a serious problem, since all forms are present to the intellect, as he has explained and will explain again. The separate discussion of digestion stages in this chapter may not fully match the chapter heading, but that is a minor point.

  199. An abscess is a large, hot swelling; a boil is a broader term and can include cold swellings.

  200. This wording suggests that the end of this digestion comes when food reaches the stomach, where another digestion also takes place. One could say that the first digestion is completed there, though it begins in the mouth: “completed” would mean perfected or brought to its fullest stage. The four stages are the four main visible transformations in a fully developed animal. In fact, food changes at every moment from the time it is chewed until it becomes part of an organ, so its transformations cannot be limited to four.

  201. The word “of” may explain which powers these are, or where they come from: they may be the governing nature itself, in its branches and stages, or powers that arise from nature.

The author would not have mistaken the role of the mesentery.

  203. This is the third place where the two powers are defined. The first definition comes from Avicenna; the second appears incidentally at the end of the division of powers; this third one is the main definition here. The phrase “in their true sense” signals that the earlier definition was only nominal, since it came before the existence of these powers was established. As Avicenna says in The Healing, definitions given before a thing's existence is proved are nominal definitions; once it is proved, the same definitions become real ones.

  204. Nourishment occurs directly, while growth occurs through nourishment. Since the nutritive power acts through three operations, some say it is only a conceptual unity: the power that gathers food, joins it to the body, and changes it into the body's substance. The fuller account is that it is one power with different aspects and stages, just as the chief of all the powers—the soul's commanding light—is one, and the other powers are its modes and expressions. As the Persian saying puts it, “In the house, all is the householder.”

  205. The phrase “natural ends” excludes ends chosen by will, since a change in chosen ends does not by itself mean a change in the one who chooses.

  206. Another proof, besides the difference in ends, is that the actions themselves differ and the two powers can operate independently. The nutritive power brings about a qualitative change, using digestion and then adhesion; it also produces the body's substantial forms. The growth power brings about a weak, gradual change in quantity.

  207. Fire changes air. An opponent could therefore say that the nutritive power is air, since both it and air “nourish”: air is said to nourish fire by changing into it. But air destroys fire by changing it into itself; otherwise the fire would rise to the sphere of ether or become earth.

  208. The point is that bodily powers, insofar as they are bodily, cannot act without limit. But insofar as they are connected to intelligible and immaterial things, they may do so: through that connection they serve as powers and instruments of those things. Still, since they are also connected to matter and body, the continued flow of intelligible forms into them depends on the recipient's continuing to exist. A recipient made of parts with opposing natures, each tending to separate from the others, cannot last forever. Otherwise those parts would be prevented from acting according to their own natures and forced to do the opposite, which is impossible according to the philosophers.

  209. Since the appeal to the body being made up of basic elements is the same as the second argument, the author says he will examine that argument.

  210. The discussion concerns the loss of the moisture supplied by food; what weakens the nutritive power is the loss of the body's innate moisture, which sustains its natural heat. There is no circle. The innate moisture declines through the weakening of the cause that sustains it. A thing disappears or weakens when the cause that keeps it present or strong is absent; it may also weaken because of some other cause, such as increased heat. Two things that depend on one another—especially when one exists in the other—may decline together, each in a different causal respect. For example, when matter loses its form, that form's individual existence ends; when the form disappears, the matter also ceases to exist. Here, the form preserves the body's material organization. As the form weakens, the material becomes less stable; that, in turn, weakens the form's activity further, though in a new degree. The process continues until the body breaks down.

    ↩

  211. The objection is that a longer period of nourishment does not help, since a natural power acts steadily and accidental causes do not simply join it. The answer is that the forces consuming moisture grow stronger because of poor care of food, air, and other necessary conditions. Even a careful, wise, medically trained person, who watches over their health and does everything they can, cannot know all the events decreed for them or ward off every stroke of chance. One may object that poor care also occurs in youth, and that nourishment repairs the damage. The reply is that such chance events weaken not only the body's mixture and the matter that receives it, but also the power and agent. The nutritive power cannot make good all the damage; it too keeps weakening. It is like someone pitching a tent in a storm that blows from every direction. Each time the wind twists the tent and threatens to bring it down, the person repairs it, raising the poles and tightening the pegs. But as the wind shakes the tent's supports, it also weakens the person doing the repairs, until the person is exhausted and the tent collapses.

    ↩

  212. Since things are naturally inclined to seek their own good and perfection, nothing acts by its nature in a way that leads to its own destruction. The natural heat's gradual drying of moisture must therefore be a form of completion. Once it has reached completion, it no longer needs that connection, so its relation to the moisture ends. Understand this if you are able, and do not be heedless.

  213. The author is considering the issue from the standpoint of divine causes; this note addresses natural causes, though it too is sound. As for the claim that semen's temperament is finer and stronger, the key is to distinguish mature, firmly established moisture from a finer temperament. Moisture, understood as a substance that binds the original organs together—especially the heart—is not the same as temperament, which is an attribute. Even if this moisture comes from semen, the argument concerns the moisture in the organs, one of the four secondary humours described by physicians. It is clearly original and innate, unlike later or foreign moisture. To deny this is unreasonable. The objection that a more balanced temperament should at once give rise to the soul's powers is also answered by the fact that the temperament of a young adult is more balanced than that of an older person, even though the latter has fuller mental powers, especially inward speech and thought. These powers do not flow into semen at the outset: it does not yet contain the heart, brain, and liver, where the three vital spirits reside. Rather, the powers and perfections flow through those spirits. Yet without semen and the original, governing organs, no such perfections would arise at all.

  214. This objection is extremely weak. Seminal moisture—the secondary moisture that binds the organs—does not disappear until death, even in a body that has become thin and fragile. Could one say that naturally moist skin, even after being soaked in water, contains no moisture of its own?

    ↩

  215. Who restricted it to those particular vessels? The issue is whether original moisture is stronger and firmer than moisture acquired later, not whether one temperament is stronger than another. What does this objection have to do with that?

  216. This is a subtle allusion. The main point is that mixing foreign moisture with moisture from food weakens its quality and makes it less like the body's own moisture. It is called a subtle allusion because the third argument says that even the best chyle cannot replace what the original organs lose: its quality is too different, not merely because it has mixed with foreign moisture.

  217. The author does not mention the “originated” being, though he is setting out to list all the rational possibilities. Here, “originated” has a broad sense: a generated thing is preceded by both matter and time, while an originated thing is not; it is the opposite of this combined condition. “Complete” and “incomplete” are not used in their usual sense of having, or lacking, a further state to reach. The author himself says that some incomplete beings are self-sufficient souls, not things made to become matter for something else. Nor are the souls of the heavenly spheres merely supposed to last forever; they are held to do so in fact. Here “complete” means a being that is not made to serve as matter or a means for another being; “incomplete” means one that does serve this role. Elsewhere, the author says that every being is either complete or incomplete, and that complete beings may be above perfection or simply perfect, while incomplete beings may or may not be self-sufficient.

  218. One might ask why a body's complete cause could not preserve its life through an endless succession of motions, just as successive motions preserve it for a time during its life. This proof and the following point about complete beings appear to form one argument: it proceeds from substantial motion to the claim that each level of a moving being has an end. Plants, animals, and human beings are levels along this motion, and the moving being must pass from one level to the next; natural death is that transition. The proof is sound, though the claim that a plant's end is to feed an animal, and an animal's end is to feed a human, needs qualification. It concerns a plant on the way to animal life, serving as its matter, and an animal on the way to human life—not a fully formed plant such as an almond tree or a complete animal such as a horse or cow. It would be strange to call a tree's becoming food for an animal its natural death, rather than an accidental death, and the same is true of animals. Keep this distinction in mind.

Likewise, if bodily powers could act without limit, the rational soul would set them aside once it reached its goal. Since the soul naturally turns toward God and is little concerned with the body, the body breaks down.

But here the organs differ by kind. Different readiness in matter cannot explain differences between kinds; the active cause, or its different aspects, must also differ. The causes must exist together, so the chain would be simultaneous, not a sequence through time.

  229. The circle and endless chain are impossible here because the things that depend on one another are active causes arranged in order, not passive materials that receive forms.

  252. A single, unified being can contain the good and perfection found in many separate beings.   322. Mulla Sadra gives a fuller answer in The Origin and the Return. One might object that the senses detect opposing qualities, such as heat and cold, not “opposition” itself, which is an idea grasped by reason. Why, then, should the number of touch powers depend on kinds of opposition? Also, sight perceives opposites such as black and white through one power. Why could touch not do the same?

    One weak answer is that the basic qualities felt by touch—heat, cold, wetness, and dryness—differ more sharply than colors, smells, and tastes, so touch needs separate powers. The better answer is this: an animal's body has a balanced mixture of these basic qualities. When one of them is opposed by what the body touches, the animal is affected. The balanced state is cold compared with pure heat and hot compared with pure cold; it is wet compared with pure dryness and dry compared with pure wetness. So the power of touch can be counted as four powers, one for each way the body can be affected by an opposing quality. It is not necessary to count separate powers for every related difference, such as rough and smooth or hard and soft. Those are effects of the basic qualities, and counting them separately would lead to far more than four. The point is that touch responds to what opposes the body's balanced state, not to qualities that match it.

  329. Today, natural philosophers and mathematicians have made deep studies of hearing, sight, and the other outer senses, supported by extensive experiments.
