  330. The person raising this objection should first ask how air ripples and takes on a shape. He seems not to have understood it, perhaps imagining that air takes the shape of letters as writing takes shape on a page. That is why he raised this objection. The rippling is more like the waves made when a stone is dropped into water; the changing quality is more like water taking on different colors in succession. For example, when someone says the Arabic word ḍaraba (“he struck”), the air ripples outward in circles, like water around a stone. As the speaker says the first sound, the air around them takes on that sound's quality, as water might turn yellow; with the next sound it takes on another quality, as if turning green; and with the last, another, as if turning red. These changing qualities spread around the speaker. The whole ripple and its quality cannot reach one person but only part of it reach another, since a quality cannot be divided in this way.

    ↩

  331. The very feature that seems to cause the problem also resolves it. Air takes on the letters in succession. Sound and speech do not persist unchanged. If the air held each letter as writing holds a shape on a page, the likeness of all its parts would indeed be a problem. But sound is not fixed either as it begins or as it continues. Each part of the similar air takes on each letter in turn. In this account, hearing does not repeat. If the air around you is warmed by your breath, then quickly cooled and returned to its usual state, does everyone nearby feel the heat over and over? No: the warmth has already vanished by the time it reaches touch. The same goes for the cold and the return to normal temperature. Apply this to the successive sounds ḍ, r, and b in ḍarb. One might object that, since there is no indivisible instant, the air's first quality lasts for some time, so each new arrival of air should make hearing repeat. But air is continuous: one part blocks another from arriving all at once, just as hearing cannot be divided into separate acts. Or, if we allow the point for the sake of argument, each quality in one stretch of air may prepare the neighboring stretch to take on the next quality. The preparation comes and goes as the new quality appears.

    ↩

  332. No one holds that the same parcel of air travels all the way from the striker to the struck object and then to the ear; this is only a far-fetched possibility. The air released by the strike at one end of a long distance cannot cut through all the air between there and the ear. The note may instead point to what we said: one stretch of air prepares the next to take on the quality, so that the quality reaches the ear without the original air itself traveling there.

    The view chosen by the author is strong and avoids the difficulties about hearing direction, nearness, and distance. It also accounts for cases that challenge the other account: people hear outside sounds with their heads under water, and can hear a stick striking the side of a water-filled basin. Ringing in the head comes from movement of inner vapors and air. We have already seen that the evidence from sound traveling in air does not prove that rippling causes sound or that transmission causes hearing. This view could also make sense of reports that Pythagoras and others heard sounds from the heavenly spheres. Still, the third and fifth pieces of evidence given earlier seem to require transmission through air. Perhaps there is another hidden condition, or some obstacle such as air that is too thin or too dense.

  337. The objection also applies to touch. As explained earlier, touch does not perceive the direction from which something came, yet what it senses is not universal. A sound, too, has particular features besides its direction. The reply is that, while touch may not perceive the direction from which a touched thing came, it does perceive the direction of the body part that carries the sense of touch. So its object is not universal.

    If hearing first perceives a nearby sound and only later, by tracing the waves, a distant one, it would perceive the same sound as both near and far. If it does not perceive the sound at the ear and has not yet traced it back to its distance, then it first hears a sound without any place or direction and so hears a universal sound. That is impossible. It would also fail to perceive the other details that make the sound particular. If it cannot perceive where the air carrying the sound is, then it cannot perceive the direction of the sound's source either.

  338. Even if the premises of this argument were proved with certainty, it would show only that a higher level of existence contains what is found in a lower one—for example, intellect and the imaginal realm contain what is found in the bodily realm. It would not prove that one body contains every perfection found in another body, even if one body is subtler and more refined than the other. In any case, the argument offered here is not a proof.

  339. I say: the view he chose about sight is a powerful one, with sound insight, and well suited to teaching and learning. Yet what the Shaykh of Illumination, al-Suhrawardi, says is also lofty and precious. It points to the soul's highest states. He explicitly says that souls are pure lights without a fixed essence, because they never stop rising beyond each level they reach. Their existence has no boundary at which it comes to rest.

    An essence is what can be bounded by a definition that includes what belongs to it and excludes what does not. It expresses a limit in existence, if existence can be limited. The author's path concerns the perceiver's union with what is directly perceived; the Shaykh's path concerns its union with what is perceived indirectly. The latter is included in the former. Union with what is directly perceived entails union with what is indirectly perceived, since things enter the mind as they are. Their essence is the same in both realms, while existence is both what distinguishes them and what they share. A single reality is multiplied only when something else, of whatever kind, intervenes between its instances.

    Illuminationist knowledge can also be stronger or weaker. The soul's knowledge of itself, its powers, and its body is all direct and present knowledge, since all of them are present to it as a thing is present to itself. This means simply that a thing is never separate from itself, though this presence can vary in strength. Even when the soul forgets its Lord and is made to forget itself, its knowledge of itself remains present knowledge. When it comes to know itself and thereby knows its Lord, that too is present knowledge. But what a difference there is between those two states!

    How could the soul fail to know things through an illuminating relation, when pure existence is the basis of the perceiver's own existence? Every being has what it is in, why it is, what it is, and whether it is. In the divine section of The Four Journeys, while explaining the saying “The perfection of knowing Him is to affirm Him,” the author says that anyone who understands the meaning of Necessary Existence—as the fullest and most complete existence, on which all possible beings with their incomplete natures depend—also understands that there must be a Necessary Existent. If there were not, nothing in the world would exist. But that conclusion is false, so its premise must be false as well. The truth of existence is known fully through direct, witnessing knowledge, because, as we established earlier, the image of a thing in knowledge must itself be the reality of the thing known.

    The author appears to limit direct, present knowledge to two cases, but that is only when the question is viewed broadly. The objections against the Shaykh can be answered.

    The first objection is answered by saying that what is material in relation to the first principles is not material in relation to those principles. The author himself cites the learned Mirdamad to this effect in the discussion of forms in the First Journey. The same can be said of the soul, considered from its hidden and more inward level.

    The second objection is answered by the Shaykh's suggestion that one of the images exists in the imaginal world. That is a reasonable view, but the author gives no reason for dismissing it.

    The third objection is answered by noting that the author's claim—that perception is only an image of a thing being present to the perceiver—requires a particular relation between them. This is contradicted by our knowledge of ourselves, where everyone agrees that knower and known are one. It is also contradicted by cases in which the author, Porphyry, and others say that the knower becomes one with what it knows. The soul has another kind of unity as well.

    The fourth objection is answered by what we have said about the name “illuminating relation.”

    I have discussed this at length even though it goes beyond the scope of these notes, because the author rejects this view in many of his works, including The Four Journeys, The Throne of Wisdom, and his notes on The Wisdom of Illumination. I have found the view true, and so I have not concealed it. I have lifted some of its veils and brought out a few of its secrets, on the condition that you keep them from those who should not hear them. God is witness between you and me.

Experience shows that perception is connected to the body and to external material things. So the questions of how an image is imprinted or how rays leave the eye still need to be studied, even after we establish that the image perceived is immaterial.

  343. A Persian verse arranges the parts of the eye in this order: the hard outer coat, the choroid, the retina, the vitreous fluid, the crystalline fluid, the arachnoid layer, the albuminous fluid, the iris, the cornea, and the joining layer. The traditional anatomy described here divides the eye into seven coats and three fluids. The hard coat begins at the end of the tough membrane around the hollow optic nerve. Anatomists say there are two membranes inside the skull around the brain, one thick and one thin, as well as an outer membrane covering the skull.

    The choroid is described as woven from the ends of the thin membrane and from veins and arteries. It is compared to the placenta because of its many vessels, or because it forms a net around the eye's contents. The retina is said to begin at the ends of the hollow optic nerve. It surrounds the vitreous and crystalline fluids and extends to the arachnoid layer, like a net holding a catch. Others say its name comes from the many vessels that pass through it from the thin membrane.

    The vitreous fluid is described as clear, thick, and slightly reddish, like melted glass. It surrounds the back half of the crystalline fluid and feeds it. Since the crystalline fluid is very white, clear, and bright, the account says it cannot be made directly from blood; the vitreous fluid serves as an intermediary. It is clear because it feeds what is clear, reddish because it comes from blood, and thick so that it does not leak away. It lies behind the crystalline fluid because its supply comes from the brain through the retina, and so it must connect to it and lie closer to its source of nourishment.

    The crystalline fluid, also called the icy fluid, is described as clear and firm like ice. It is the eye's most important part, where sight occurs; the other parts serve and protect it. It is placed in the center because of its importance and is compared to a mirror in which images form. The arachnoid layer is said to be extremely thin, like a spider's web, and to cover the front of the crystalline fluid. It begins at the retina and separates the crystalline fluid from the albuminous fluid, which is excess nourishment. Constant contact with this excess would be harmful, so the layer is thin enough not to block light or images from reaching the crystalline fluid.

    The albuminous fluid is described as resembling egg white in color, clarity, and thickness. It lies in front of the crystalline fluid to soften strong light before it reaches it, keep it moist so air does not dry it out, and protect it from the roughness of the iris. The iris is described as a thick layer, hard on the outside and soft and sponge-like on the inside. Its central opening faces the crystalline fluid and lets light through, like the hole left when a grape is pulled from its stem. The iris also holds the albuminous fluid in place and keeps debris from reaching the pupil. Aristotle is said to have considered the eye's natural color black, because black gathers and strengthens sight and moderates light. Galen is said to have favored blue, arguing that black compresses the visual spirit too much while blue, with its whiteness, spreads it out and strengthens sight. The note adds that Aristotle supposedly had dark eyes and Galen very blue ones.

    The cornea is described as a hard, clear layer like white horn thinned by scraping. It begins at the hard outer coat and protects the layers and fluids beneath it. It is said to have four layers, like horn, so that if one is damaged, the others still protect the eye. It is clear so that light can pass through, like the glass of a lantern that protects the flame without blocking its light. The joining layer is described as a firm, clear, cartilage-like covering, connected to muscles and containing soft white tissue that lubricates the eye and eyelid and keeps them from drying out as they move. Hippocrates is said to trace it to the outer membrane over the skull, while Rufus traces it to the inner tough membrane. Unlike the other layers, it joins around the cornea rather than covering it; the note says that this is why it is called the joining layer. The account says these details are stated in medical works.

The intellect's use of imagination for matters that are not sensed is another obstacle; illness can remove it. The author means this second kind of position: the body's own arrangement, which is part of its existence. Even if he also means an outside relation, such as nearness, the reasoning can still be followed: making an effect depends on existence, and a body's existence depends on an arrangement that connects it with what surrounds it, so its effect also requires a suitable outside relation, such as nearness.

  379. I say that the argument is strong. Matter and form, though both kinds of substance, are not a body by themselves. Their combination becomes one, forming a new kind of thing: a body. In the same way, the whiteness we see and the sweetness we taste do not by themselves ground the judgment that “this sugar is sweet.” Nor is their real combination enough. Combining things is the work of a power that acts, not one that perceives—just as wood can join one thing to another without being aware that it has done so. The judgment itself is the perception of the real combination. Judgment is a kind of knowledge: perceiving that a relation does or does not hold. This particular judgment, the perception of how these qualities come together, belongs to common sense, not to intellect at its higher level, since intellect does not perceive or judge particulars there. Even if intellect does perceive particulars, it does so at its lower level, the level of the senses. The power that judges particulars at that level is common sense. If intellect perceived particular sensible things at its higher level, there would be no need for the senses.

  401. If this argument worked, it would show that estimation is intellect restricted to particular things. But it does not. Affection, one of the things estimation perceives, is not merely an abstract relation with no individual instances, nor is it a general kind that has only one instance. There are many particular affections: a person’s love for a child, an animal’s love for its young, or a donkey’s attachment to something. One person may love a child, a spouse, and many other things; a thousand distinct affections may arise in a single day. These inclinations, longings, and affections are particular meanings that exist in the soul: they were not there, then came to be, and later pass away.

    A particular meaning of this kind must be perceived in relation to what it is about. The outer senses, common sense, and imagination cannot perceive it, since they perceive and preserve images, while affection and hostility are meanings. Intellect cannot perceive them either, since it perceives universals, while these are particular experiences. Their particularity is not merely a matter of being related to something. So there must be a power besides sense, imagination, and intellect. This is what philosophers mean by estimation. Intellect sees no difference in kind between whiteness and affection as general kinds that can have many instances. The difference is that whiteness has particular visible instances, while affection has particular inwardly experienced instances. The same goes for hostility, dislike, and similar feelings.

    The author’s reasoning depends on two claims. First, affection and hostility have no true particular instances of their own; they are only general relations attached to particular images. This is not so. In his discussion of will and aversion in Theology, he himself says that will and aversion are psychic qualities, like other mental qualities, and are known inwardly, like pleasure and pain. Their particular instances are easy to recognize. He adds that perceiving particular instances of each is linked to perceiving particular instances of other things.

    Second, the argument assumes that animals without reason perceive particular meanings that are only relations by having their imagination connect with the governing forms of their kinds. Since they have no intellect, their estimation would then be intellect restricted to particulars. If this idea were meant to deny that evil has a real existence—some philosophers say evil is only incidental in the divine order—it should be limited to mistaken estimation, such as wrongly judging that a yellow object is honey or being afraid of a dead person. It should not be extended to a trained dog’s estimation, a parent’s love, trust, or fear of a dangerous enemy.

    If the reason for not treating these meanings as a separate realm is that they are not distinct from the images imagination perceives, that would be an arbitrary rule. One could just as well say they belong to a lower spiritual realm, since they are particular meanings in souls connected to spiritual and physical forms, or to a higher realm because of their nobility. I suspect the author was driven by his deep commitment to unity. Since inward meanings do not have the many visible forms, positions, places, and directions found in physical images, it was easier to treat them as one. Yet their subjects and times still differ. Strikingly, the author says this in several places, including The Keys to the Unseen.

    ↩

  402. There are obvious problems here. The intellect’s recognition of a meaning does not require another power to perceive its opposite. Sight and touch often make mistakes, and the intellect judges that what they perceive is false. Nor do we accept that hostility must be sensed if it is present in an individual. We do not sense bodyhood, unity, or existence with any of the five senses; the senses perceive only a body’s qualities. The author’s proof may be weak, but there is another way to question whether estimation is a separate power. Sensible things are perceived by common sense after they have first been present to the outer senses, such as sight, hearing, and touch. The soul knows these things directly through a kind of union with the bodily powers. In the same way, our ordinary, representational knowledge of inner meanings such as affection and hostility may be preceded by the soul’s direct awareness of them. Why could common sense not perceive these inner qualities, just as it perceives external qualities? The fact that they are called meanings, in contrast to images, because qualities such as heat and blackness can belong to things outside the soul and body, does not prove that they require another independent power. Consider this carefully. If common sense is enough to perceive meanings, then imagination may also be enough to preserve them, and there may be no need for a separate memory power.

  406. “The soul is all the powers” does not mean that the soul is merely their sum, since a sum has no separate existence or unity. It does not mean that two things become one, or that the soul leaves one level to take on another. Rather, the soul is the source that remains present at every level: the spirit behind spirits and the form behind forms. It does not leave its higher level when it takes on the features of a lower one, nor does it leave its lower level behind when it develops into a more complete one. This happens through the soul’s own development and change in its being. It has many powers in one, and one soul through many powers. Its existence is one, though the ideas we form from its different levels are not all the same.

  407. This is also an argument from what we know. What we know is something we want or value, and the one who judges must have both sides before them. But if the one who knows what is desirable were not also the one moved to want it, knowledge would not give rise to desire, and desire would not give rise to knowledge. That is not so. So the one who knows and the one who desires are one.

    ↩

  408. The ideas we draw from the soul’s powers are not all the same. Each action has its own name and meaning.

    ↩

  409. One might say that this third argument adds nothing, since it is obvious that the soul perceives sensible things. I reply that the argument is not about ordinary, image-based perception. Many people think that this perception belongs to the body’s organs, not the soul. But direct awareness of the body and its powers does belong to the soul. It must happen without an instrument; otherwise, another instrument would be needed to perceive the first one, and the process would never end. So one soul, in different states, perceives both particular things and general ideas.

  410. This can be challenged. The argument assumes, without proof, that the body cannot be a place for desire or anger. Another factor might prevent a desire or anger from arising in a particular part of the body.

  411. The argument shows that desire and anger are immaterial powers, but not by itself that they are the soul. They could belong to another immaterial power.   412. This objection is fair. The claim assumes that the brain’s vital spirit has no more capacity to hold images than any other body, but there is no proof of that.

  413. If the imagined size is an immaterial, imaginal form, and imagination is one with what it imagines, then this already proves that imagination is immaterial at the imaginal level.

  414. If Avicenna allowed that the soul creates an image rather than receiving an imprint, this conclusion would not follow. The soul is also immaterial at the imaginal level.

  415. This is based on Avicenna’s rejection of change in a thing’s essence and of the soul’s becoming one with intellect after first becoming one with sense. He does not reject the claim that existence is real in the world or that it can become stronger and weaker.

  416. This applies especially to the vital spirit. If a body or bodily thing could perceive, it would be the most likely place for perception, since the powers are said to exist in it as qualities or forms.   417. There is another possibility: one image could be formed in the original part only. The author does not mention it because a new part would have to take the place of one that broke down, and the replacement should have the same form as what it replaces.

  418. “Separate sources” here means the soul that is spread through the heavens. Separate intellects cannot contain particular images. Since the author means the soul in the heavens, he raises the question only about the soul.

  419. The text may originally have read: “Just as when the soul gains the ability to connect with intellect, it can recover images from the active intellect after they fade, so it can do the same here.” The copies I have seen read as printed.

  420. A copy made in 1211 AH reads: “When the soul gains the ability to connect with intellect, and the images fade, it can recover them from the active intellect.”

  421. There is no problem on the right account. At the imaginal level, the soul is immaterial in a way that allows it to take on imaginal forms. The difficulty is how these images are made present to the soul, not how they are physically lodged in it.

  422. The words “although it is” should be removed from the sentence.

  423. People may think general ideas come from the heart or brain because they meet them clothed in words and sensible images. But general ideas are immaterial. When a person understands one, the immaterial self takes in all its outward and inward instances. No pine-shaped heart, sticky brain, or bodily spirit could do this.

  424. The individual parts of the body do not truly hear, see, or speak as a person does. “The whole” here means the physical body, which many people think is the human being.   425. Even someone who believes that images are physically imprinted can answer this objection. Position and place may belong to the image’s existence without belonging to its definition. The fire imagined in the mind does not burn, and imagining a straight line does not make the mind straight.

  426. The author’s wording is surprising. Mental existence includes both imagined forms and intellectual ideas; both are called what they are in a basic sense, not in the ordinary sense. A mental sphere is not an ordinary material sphere. It is an imaginal or intellectual form.

The author does not use the distinction between these two ways of saying “square,” though it appears often in his books, and the people making the argument have missed it.

  428. This refers to “not made of matter.”

  429. The forms made by the soul are the source from which the heavenly spheres come.

  430. Calling the knowledge of higher, immaterial sources “conceptions” is not exact. Their knowledge is direct; it is not made up of ideas and judgments in the ordinary sense.

  431. There is no matter here to receive a new form, as wax receives the shape of a square. Giving an image a specific identity is not a second act added to its creation. The defining feature follows from the image itself.

  432. This is like the forms of the afterlife, which do not have the place and position found in this world.

  433. Changes in the next world do not happen because matter takes on one form after another. There is no matter there. Changes such as new skins or new kinds of pleasure come from one creation followed by another. The details will be discussed in the sections on the afterlife.

  434. When an imagined form disappears, it does not turn into something else that can serve as its matter. It simply ceases to be. This is different from material things, which change into something else.

  435. The distinction between images in the world of imagination does not mean they have positions in the physical world. This note corrects the wording of the sentence it follows.

  436. The relation is part of what makes a particular instance what it is; it is not an added thing alongside it. If the relation were an extra object, the difference between the general kind and the particular instance would not be only a matter of thought. This also challenges the argument that estimation perceives a compound of meaning and image. If you ask how estimation can link a meaning to an image without knowing the image, the answer is like saying that Zayd is a human being: it is not a real joining of two separate things. The image is perceived by imagination; the particular meaning is perceived by intellect linked to imagination, or by estimation in the usual account. The relation makes it particular.

  437. Hostility joined to a particular image is not one single thing. It is perceived by intellect working with imagination, not by intellect connected to imagination alone. This also challenges the argument just given.

  438. The power of resolve is the firm wish of practical reason, such as deciding to visit someone who is ill. Animal desire is the firm wish of the bodily motive power, such as visiting someone for personal gain. In a human being, theoretical and practical reason play roles like perception and movement in an animal. The higher source of an inclination is called will or love; the animal source is called appetite. Religious language also distinguishes them. Mystics sometimes use “love” of God and the soul, though prophets usually teach with simpler, proper terms.

    The author identifies will with the power that wills, as he identifies knowledge with the one who knows. Both estimation and imagination are immaterial, but estimation is at a higher level. The note that no one calls the power that urges action material is meant as a small exception to praise, a familiar figure of speech.

  439. The philosophers’ classification of ability as a mental quality supports the author’s account that the soul is one through all its levels, reaching into the body.

  440. The working power spreads through the body much like nature does. It acts through the muscles and limbs, while nature acts through simple and complex bodies.

  441. These thinkers may have spoken about life without separating it into perception and movement. Yet they did, in effect, understand animal life through both. Those who followed the path of life also included perception and movement in their account, but did not treat them as separate paths.

  442. This can be read as “a substance moved by itself,” or as meaning that the soul is a self-moving substance. In the author’s interpretation, this means the changing nature that is one level of the soul.

  443. The copies I have seen read this way, though I cannot check Avicenna’s text now. “And some said” would be a clearer transition: those who did not avoid calling the soul a body divided into several groups, including those who said it was made of indivisible particles.

  444. Here “source” means the source of the world, though some thinkers made it a source only through the first source, God. Thales of Miletus is said to have called water the first element, containing the forms of everything that exists or could exist. From it, earth formed by thickening and freezing, while fire and air formed by thinning. The sky, some said, came from smoke rising from fire. A story attributed to the Torah says that God created a substance, looked upon it, and its parts melted into water. Vapor rose from the water and formed the heavens; foam appeared on its surface and formed the earth and mountains. Similar stories appear in reports from the Imams. Other thinkers said that earth came first, or that air did, becoming fire when thin and earth when dense. Some named fire or vapor as the first source. Anaxagoras spoke of a mixture. Democritus proposed small, hard particles in an endless empty space. Dualists said light and darkness were the world’s two roots. Some Iranian thinkers proposed five eternal things: God, soul, matter, time, and empty space. The Pythagoreans said numbers came from unity and were the source of things.

    These views are false if taken literally, though many can be understood in a better way. Their argument can be set out like this: the soul perceives other things; anything that perceives other things is a source; every source is fire, air, earth, or water; so the soul is one of these. The same pattern lies behind the other views.

    ↩

  445. These thinkers counted the four elements as the roots of the world’s coming to be and continuing to exist. The world arises from them, while its survival depends on drawing what is useful and driving away what is harmful, through what they called Love and Strife.

    ↩

  446. These thinkers treated life as their route to the soul, and explained it through what gives life, supports it, prepares for it, or follows from it.

    ↩

  447. For these thinkers, the soul changes only in its qualities: it gains more knowledge, power, and similar features, while its underlying nature remains fixed. The author’s view is different. Through substantial movement, the soul itself changes in its being, while one underlying thread remains from its beginning to its end. This follows from his view that existence is what is real, and that what makes a thing distinct from others is the same as what makes it continuous through change. So the soul’s level as a potential intellect and its level as an actual intellect belong to one changing soul.

    The difference between a Prophet and the rest of the community is therefore a difference in the soul’s being, not merely in outside qualities. If such a difference exists within one soul, the difference between two souls may be greater still—like the difference between spirit and body, or between the spirit that gives itself up in the light of the One and the body it leaves behind.

    ↩

  448. In this account, every earlier form becomes like the material for the final, most complete form. The final form gathers and completes what came before. At the inner level, individuals of the human kind may therefore differ as kinds: some are intellects only in possibility, others are intellects in reality. The rising intellects relate to the final, perfected intellect as earlier forms relate to the final form. In one sense, they are that intellect, and it is them. The author points to sayings about the Prophet and the Imams: “You are remembered among those who remember; your names among the names; your selves among the selves; your spirits among the spirits; your bodies among the bodies.” He also cites the saying that a believer is a mirror for another believer.

    ↩

  449. The author has briefly pointed to the Prophet’s spiritual reality as the highest completion, for whose sake the rest was created. In this spiritual aspect, no angel or prophet equals him, since every soul and intellect comes from that source. He then turns to the Prophet’s ordinary human life, where likeness and comparison apply. A true knower must hold together both levels: the image and the meaning, the human form and its spiritual reality. The Qur'an says, “If We had made him an angel, We would have made him a man,” to avoid both exaggerating his status and denying the high rank of holy souls.

    What is said about the Prophets and Imams—their purity and their likeness to God—is true of their spiritual aspect. What is said about their human limits is also true of their bodily aspect. They eat, drink, sleep, and receive knowledge from Gabriel, because all their gifts come from God. Yet the body’s physical nature is overwhelmed by their spiritual nature. This is why it is said that the Prophet cast no shadow, saw behind him, and that the body of a believer does not decay.

    ↩

  450. Even a heavenly body, considered only as a body, can perish. The source of its motion is its soul or nature, which is outside the body when “body” means matter considered on its own. The soul and nature are not outside the body when body is considered together with its form.

    ↩

  451. The soul’s original nature must lead it toward its goal. Otherwise, this natural drive would be pointless. The goal of living souls is something lasting: God and the immaterial intellects, or the world of imagined and estimative forms. These remain through God’s lasting existence.

    ↩

  452. Movement can be divided into six kinds. Three begin from outside the moving thing: movement through place may begin because something is uncomfortable; the changes in mixed bodies depend on outside heat, cold, or moisture; and the movement of simple elements depends on the conditions around them. The changing nature within a body also moves by itself, but the conflicting elements destroy one another. The other three kinds are the movements of souls. They come from within and do not conflict with one another, so they continue.

    ↩

  453. The sphere stands for the simple shape of imagined bodies. Its roundness is also explained by the way soul and body are joined as form and matter. Here “body” means a heavenly body, not an imaginal body.

  454. This seems to conflict with the earlier claim that the particles breathed in are imaginal forms, since breathing brings in the bodily vital spirit. The reply is that the vital spirit carries the powers and displays the imaginal forms. Without it, the soul’s image would have no bodily appearance. So refreshing the vital spirit also refreshes the forms it carries.

    A clearer reading is that the earlier thinkers meant imaginal bodies by “indivisible spheres,” while by what is breathed in they meant the vital spirit. They may instead have followed the theory of small, hard particles.

  455. This explains the “fire with three branches”: a body has length, width, and depth. The author also links the body’s attachment to the natural world with the fire of punishment in the next life.

  456. There is another way to interpret the number sequence. The first source is one and has no separate definition beyond its unity. From it comes the first intellect, which has two aspects: existence and essence. From that comes the soul, which has a third relation, its direction toward and care for matter. From the soul comes nature, which adds a fourth relation: being present in and acting directly on matter. This completes the active sources.

    ↩

  457. Potential intellect is like the matter of ideas, and sense is like the matter of sensible forms. Each is suited to receive its own kind, just as silver is suited to take the shape of what is made from it.

    ↩

  458. The soul does not become one with an object merely because the object is seen or understood indirectly. It becomes one with the form it directly perceives. This does not mean that the soul is made up of many parts. The forms it knows are present through the soul’s own being. As the soul becomes more complete, it gathers more things while becoming more simple.

    ↩

  459. This differs from the usual view of philosophers and natural scientists, who say that the vital spirit is made from the finest bodily fluids. The body’s organs, they say, are made from the thicker fluids. The author’s view is like his account of food: some things come from the soul itself, or from a natural power that obeys the soul. Other bodily powers may resist it and cause fatigue.

    ↩

  460. The soul is nourished by ideas and grows stronger through them. When its life appears in the body, bodily things nourish and strengthen that life. The soul rises toward the highest realm until it can stand before God. In the body, its power appears as growth, movement, and reproduction. Each soul helps produce another like itself, so life continues. In this way, all forms in the lower world are shadows of lights and qualities in the higher world.

    ↩

  461. The source of all things has three levels: God, the existence that flows from Him, and the limited forms that result. The source itself is beyond being a substance or a quality. Earlier thinkers may have meant that God is present in things through His action, not as a separate thing alongside them. Since His action is His command and light, they spoke as if He were nature, soul, or intellect in each thing. But care is needed: each level must be kept distinct and placed in its proper role.

    ↩

  462. Here “source” means the thing that gives a movement, not a second object of a verb.

    ↩

  463. The point is that every moving thing needs a source, but not always in the same way. A change in an outer feature needs something to cause that movement. A change in the thing’s very being needs something to give it existence. In this kind of movement, the changing being itself is its movement; the source does not first make it exist and then add movement to it. In outward movement, the source gives the thing existence and also causes the added movement. In either case, all movement needs a source, and the chain of moving things ends at a source that does not move.

    ↩

  464. The word “change” here is used broadly. In the usual terms, it means change in quality. Change in a thing’s substance is called coming-to-be, as explained earlier.

    ↩

  465. Substantial movement does not mean that a thing’s definition changes at every moment. Avicenna treats a changing essence as if it became an entirely different kind of thing at each moment. But the definition can remain fixed while the thing’s existence flows and changes. The whole natural world, from the heavens down to the earth, is renewed in its being. This is how the author joins the changing nature of the world with the claim that its definitions do not change.

    ↩

  466. The movement must be one individual existence unfolding through time; otherwise, there could be no gradual change. Its definition can remain one, like the definition of a human being, even though that definition is expressed through many distinct beings.

    ↩

  467. Separate intellects do not change. They are complete and do not wait to become something else. Change is possible in kinds of substance that depend on matter.

    ↩

  468. The highest general kind, such as substance, does not turn into another general kind. Nor does a specific kind of substance turn into another kind during ordinary gradual change. But many kinds of change can take a thing beyond its kind: a color may weaken until it is no longer that color, and a human soul may develop until it becomes angel-like or decline until it becomes devil-like or beast-like.

    ↩

  469. When the mind is only potential intellect, it receives ideas. When it connects with the active intellect, it can create and preserve them. Or “receiving” may simply mean that the soul is described as having an idea; on either reading, one thing does not have to be both receiver and creator in the same way.

  470. The two parts can each be understood because the condition for understanding applies to them; the whole cannot be understood in that way once the condition is missing. The contrast may be between the whole before division and a part afterward, or between their identities and their accidental features. Either way, if understanding required division, it would require the opposite of what it needs.

    ↩

  471. If understanding depended on division, then every intelligible thing would have to be divisible. But some intelligible things are simple and cannot be divided.

    ↩

  472. A part of a magnitude is one particular portion of it, while a particular thing can carry its whole kind. The two objections here may be one or two arguments. Either way, if a smaller part were enough to contain the form, the supposed form would be present with features unrelated to what it is. It would always be understood together with something that does not help complete its meaning.

    ↩

  473. The questioner points to a mistaken reversal: every division into measured parts gives similar parts, but not every division into similar parts is a division of size. Dividing a universal into its particular kinds is an example.

  474. The phrase about adding “rational” to “animal” may sound as if human and horse natures differ, even though the questioner says their animal nature is the same. The reply is that adding a different feature forms a new kind; it does not split one reality into physical pieces. A universal kind is never found outside its particular instances as one separate thing. Even in the mind, its divisions are made by considering it in different ways. If it were literally divided, its parts would have size.

    ↩

  475. This would also require an accident to move from one subject to another.

    ↩

  476. These souls may not yet understand in a fully intellectual way, but they have a capacity close to understanding. If divine care gives them a true intellectual form, they must be ready to receive it, since gifts follow the recipient’s capacity.

    ↩

  477. Most people cannot understand a universal as a purely intellectual existence, shared equally by many instances. They picture it as an extended thing covering its instances, much as they picture existence as a beam of light. This comes from the strength of imagination and the weakness of their developing intellect. People trained in theory or practice can correct these images with reason. For many, “immaterial” means only that something is not material; a few understand it as a nature stripped of all accompanying features.

  478. The author’s account seems to distinguish three things: a particular idea perceived by sense or imagination; a universal in the strict philosophical sense; and an indeterminate idea that can be considered in different ways. Philosophers usually mean the second when they speak of universals. If minds genuinely understand a universal that is free of particular limits, this understanding is immaterial, though immateriality itself has degrees. The author’s account may deny ordinary people the highest degree of this understanding, but it cannot deny that universal ideas exist in our minds.

    ↩

  479. The argument moves from number to other realities and then to intellectual forms. The fact that ten can be divided does not prove that other things, especially intellectual forms, can be divided. Ten is divisible because it is a multitude of units; bodies are divisible because they have matter. The argument concerns universal ten as understood by the intellect, not an endless series of individual tens.

    ↩

  480. Ten is not identical with the many units that compose it, though it can be understood as made up of them. Its meaning as a number includes unity.

    ↩

  481. The problem with Avicenna’s claim about multitude and unity has already been discussed. In his examples, unity itself includes the multiplicity of parts. That is why some philosophers say that division belongs to the thing represented, not to the feature that represents it.

    ↩

  482. If “division” means actual separation, the body itself is not what is divided; matter is. If it means division in thought, magnitude is what is directly divisible, and the body is divisible through it.

    ↩

  483. Even if body and unity refer to one thing, they do not have the same features. A body exists and produces effects; its unity is what rules out division and generality. Different descriptions of one thing can carry different features. The better reply is that, if unity is only a way we consider a thing, it does not literally reside in the body.

    ↩

  484. Self-knowledge may be direct: the self is both what knows and what is known. Or it may be knowledge through an image. If so, the image is either a likeness, a mere trace, or a description made from features and effects. The respondent rejects some of these options, but the answer does not rule out knowing oneself through one’s features. The clearest answer is that we know our particular self directly, as the “I” we point to; any other image or description is different from that identity.

    ↩

  485. Here, “awareness is the effect itself” treats the word “awareness” as the form present in the mind. The wording is a technical point: if awareness is the same as the effect, the next phrase adds nothing.

    ↩

  486. This assumes that “by” means “because of.” The question is whether awareness is the self’s presence itself or a separate awareness caused by an effect.

    ↩

  487. Avicenna’s point is that our own self is present through its individual identity and nature. The active intellect, by contrast, is present to us only through its nature, not as that individual being. This is direct knowledge of ourselves, but knowledge of the active intellect through an idea.

    ↩

  488. I think the reply is sound, given its assumptions: separate intellects have distinct natures, and we can know them through concepts. Knowledge through a concept differs from direct awareness, which is the very presence of what is known. A possible being's nature remains recognisable across its different ways of existing. We may therefore understand and define that nature even when we cannot fully grasp the thing's particular existence.

    The intellect can understand not only general kinds but also immaterial individuals. Knowing a separate intellect's kind, however, is not the same as possessing that intellect's own individual existence. The same nature can be present in our minds as an intelligible form without becoming the very separate being we know. Its kind may have only one individual outside the mind; that does not prevent its nature from being understood by another mind.

    A similar distinction applies when we know God through His names and attributes. We can form ideas that truly point to Him—for example, that He is existence without limitation, simple and undivided, knowing all things through Himself, and fully powerful. Such ideas express what the names mean. They are not God's own existence present in our minds. Just as God's reality is existence itself, so the concept of existence can serve, in our thought, somewhat as an essence serves for a possible being. The divine names and attributes can also play that role. A concept may be general even if its real object cannot be multiplied: the mind can consider several instances of what in fact has only one.

    It is true that members of one material kind differ through matter and its features. But what receives a form need not always be a material body. In the case of intellects, the knowing mind is the receiver. Two minds can therefore share knowledge of one nature without becoming one individual intellect. That is a different question from whether what is understood is itself a substance.

    If, instead, we reject conceptual knowledge of the intellects and allow only direct awareness of them, the situation changes. Then many souls could be directly aware of one and the same intellect. Their awareness would not be many separate copies of it, because in direct awareness what is known is present rather than represented by another image. Yet direct knowledge itself comes in degrees: the soul's awareness of itself when its intellect is only a possibility is not the same as the awareness it reaches when its intellect is fully developed and, in knowing itself, it knows its Lord.

    Nor should we be satisfied with loose, general descriptions of the intellects. We can identify the first intellect as an immaterial substance, the first thing produced by God, the cause of the second intellect, or the object sought by the soul of the highest sphere. Someone might say these are only effects, not the intellect's nature. But the reply is that they point to the inner principle from which those effects follow, just as a human being's distinctive nature is the source of reasoning and speech rather than simply those acts themselves. — س ره

    ↩

  499. The questioner is now arguing that animal souls are immaterial. The author agrees with the basic point, in keeping with his account of complete animals, and answers only the weakest part of the objection.

  500. A living being has a soul, and the organ contains an image that corresponds to that soul.   504. The author’s distinctive claim is that what makes an idea an individual also makes it universal. This is as striking as the claim attributed to Aristotle that what makes opposites alike can also keep them apart.

  505. The idea’s wide intellectual existence lets it apply to many things. Its nature by itself is neither universal nor particular, but it can be applied to many. Applying a concept to many things is a way of thinking about it, not an extra object inside it.

  506. By a “pure human being” the author does not mean the bare idea of human nature emptied of everything, even existence. He means the full intellectual reality of a human being, free from all that is alien to it: boundaries, defects, and limitations. It has none of what does not belong to human reality, and contains everything that does belong to it. As the verse says, “It is no strange thing for God to gather a world in one.”

    Although that reality embraces all the countless human individuals found outside the mind or considered within it, it remains one simple reality. Matter and its conditions—place, time, and the like—are what make the individuals many. Once those limiting conditions are removed, the general reality is not divided by them.

    Consider whiteness without referring it to this object or that object, this time or that time. Taken simply as whiteness, it is one. So it is with the pure intellectual reality of humanity: we cannot distinguish separate examples inside what is pure in this way.

    All these simple and undivided realities resemble, in their own lesser ways, the simple truth and unity of existence itself, which is the most complete of all. The author specifies particular bodily position because there is no problem with a more general concept of position being applied at the intellectual level, as he will argue later when responding to al-Ṭūsī.

  571. The “spirit” may mean Gabriel, with whom the human rational soul becomes united after changes and growth in its very being. On that reading, what is said of Gabriel also helps explain the perfected human soul. The Throne is greater than this spirit because it stands for all-embracing mercy and the divine gift of existence. Gabriel is one of the bearers of the Throne.

    The statement that the spirit could swallow the heavens means that the heavens are like a ring in a vast open country compared with the world of intellect. Gabriel also has a true form, in which the Prophet is said to have seen him twice, filling the two horizons, and an appearance suited to the human beings who see him—such as the form of Diḥya al-Kalbī in the Prophet's time.

    Gabriel is said to stand on the right of the Throne because the right stands for the stronger side, and immaterial beings belong to higher levels of existence. On this symbolic map, the holy intellects occupy the upper right, universal souls the lower right, independent imaginal forms the upper left, and universal natures the lower left. Gabriel's intercession for those who affirm God's oneness means bringing them from what they are capable of becoming to what they actually achieve. What is now an inward change will appear as intercession in the life to come.

    There is another possible reading. The spirit may be the human spirit itself, and the greater Throne may mean the full order of divine knowledge or the heart of a perfected human being, which is called God's Throne. The statement then resembles praise expressed in a form that sounds like a qualification. The perfected soul contains the higher heavens within its own existence, to say nothing of their imaginal and physical counterparts. As a Persian verse puts it, there are heavens within the realm of the soul that govern the heavens of this world.

    Another poet pictures a bird that takes in thorns with the whole rose garden and finds what is bitter sweet. The point is that the perfected soul can contain the signs of divine gentleness and divine power together. Its “form” is not merely an outward shape: it is what makes it fully what it is. Its “face” may indicate the imaginal appearance closest to its true being, a form corresponding to the human form. Its place on the right has the same symbolic meaning as before.

    The soul also intercedes by displaying a reflected form of divine unity. It gathers qualities that point to God's transcendence and qualities that point to His presence in creation, making the truth of oneness easier for others to understand. Its light burns with such force that ordinary bodily appearance veils it. As another line suggests, the sun appears in human form with its face covered. God knows best.

  588. The lamp is the light of God's oneness. The comparison with the heart's tapering shape is fitting. The heart of a believer who understands is a world of intellect that mirrors the world outside. We can picture the order of existence as a cone of light: its narrow point is towards God, and its broad base towards matter. Nearer God, oneness and simplicity are clearer; nearer matter, multiplicity and composition increase.

    In the report, the unbeliever's heart is described as dark because the world is, for that person, like a cone of darkness. It is turned upside down because attention rests on the many things of the bodily world without turning towards the unity that gathers them, and on outward forms without reaching their deeper meaning.

    A commentator distinguishes several kinds of unbelief. Some people have not received the prophetic message, or have not understood parts of it. He calls this unbelief through ignorance and says that many of these people, because of their limited opportunity, may not be punished. Others hear the message but reject it through pride, inherited loyalties, or prejudice: this is deliberate rejection. Still others affirm the message outwardly, perhaps to protect their lives or property, while denying it inwardly: this is hypocrisy, which the commentator regards as more serious.

    A further case is someone who privately accepts the truth but refuses to admit it, out of envy, stubbornness, or deference to others. The commentator treats this as a different kind of concealment. Another person may affirm the message in speech and belief yet misunderstand it because of poor judgment or misleading teachers. This is error, and its seriousness varies with the extent of the error.

    Lastly, a person may understand and accept the message yet disobey its commands while recognising the wrong. Some texts also use “unbelief” for this kind of wrongdoing. The commentator notes that other schools disagree over whether a grave sinner should be called an unbeliever, a believer, or neither. He does not treat every case as deserving the same judgment or punishment.

    The image of the dark, inverted heart can cover these different cases. Hypocrisy receives a separate image—the heart bound as if to a stake—because the person keeps the inner denial concealed while presenting the opposite outwardly. Someone who knows the truth but rejects it openly is different in that respect. The report's heart with two faces corresponds to the self that reproaches itself, pulled between contrary tendencies. — س ره

  600. The claim that the soul has only one level means, on the opposing view, that it remains numerically the same with no inward movement or change in its very existence. The author also holds that one soul has many levels, but for him these are stages of one developing being. The soul can show the qualities of the natural world, even of basic matter, and can also take on the qualities associated with God. Between those extremes lie many stages.

    The Qur'anic verse speaks of a time that passed “over the human being.” This wording suggests that even the stage of bare matter, and not only the stages of plant or animal life, can belong to the history of a human soul. That is not surprising if we mean matter and nature as stages along a person's own path of development. It would be surprising if we meant a plant, animal, or piece of matter standing outside that path, with no such movement. Considered in themselves, those separate things are not stages of this human being.

    The author gives one possible meaning of the verse. A higher reading is that it refers to the human being's prior existence in the divine realm. There, the fixed reality of a human being belonged to the level of God's names and attributes and was known directly through His knowledge. The “time” mentioned in the verse is like the “time” in the Prophet's saying, “I have a time with God.” It does not mean an ordinary period measured by clocks. The person did not yet exist through a separate existence of their own. Rather, all these realities were present through God's existence. There was not yet the scattered multitude of limited, material beings we see here.

    Even in the lower worlds, light prevails over darkness, mercy comes before anger, and unity has precedence over multiplicity. But those signs are far from the undivided reality of that earlier divine level.

  602. Views on the soul’s beginning can be sorted into two broad camps. Those who say it comes to be disagree about whether it existed before the body, began with the body, or was created through the body so that the body’s coming to be is also its own. Those who say it is eternal may mean that it is eternal by nature, as in the extreme view that the soul is God; eternal in time but created in its nature; eternal among many bodies, as those who believe in souls moving between bodies say; or eternal in a higher chain of existence as a universal intellect. The last view is Plato’s.

    ↩

  603. The heavens were thought by some philosophers to be eternal, though subject to weakness as their positions change; Sadra also says their substance changes. The point is: even if the soul were eternal, its immaterial nature would make it complete and free of weakness.

    ↩

  604. One could object that species reproduced over generations are eternal and have many individuals. The reply is that what matters is not eternity but being free of changing accidents that create many individuals. The kind survives by one individual following another; it is not one eternal individual.

    ↩

  605. The point is that this is not a feature found in every case. We should not object that the celestial bodies, too, each have a kind limited to one individual: having only one individual is not a feature reserved for immaterial beings.

    There is another answer, one that follows the author's philosophy and that of the leading sages. The heavenly spheres and the kinds of things that reproduce are coming into being and passing away in their very substance. Their existence changes at every moment. What looks like one lasting individual is, in reality, a continuous succession of stages, each coming after the disappearance of what preceded it and passing away before what follows.

    A natural kind, considered generally, has no existence apart from the individuals that embody it. Each individual comes to be; the kind therefore comes to be through them. The whole collection has no further existence in addition to the existence of its members. There are two different kinds of multiplicity: the many separate individuals of a kind, and the continuous succession of stages within each apparent individual.

    On this view, having many individuals that share one kind is a common feature of bodily and changing things. A newly occurring thing is one whose very being is renewed. What is eternal in the strict sense remains the same in itself and awaits no future development. That applies to God and to what belongs to His own reality. — س ره

    ↩

  606. “Perfect souls” may mean souls that reach the afterlife or souls that have a mode of existence before nature. In truth, a prior mode belongs to a soul that also has a later one. If all things have earlier modes in relation to their source, this is not enough to call them eternal; only the human soul can pass through to higher modes. Potentiality can be treated as the thing itself when it is ready to become actual.

    ↩

  607. The cause is the complete definition of its effect, and the effect is an incomplete expression of its cause. A lower reality is a weaker form of a higher one. The higher reality remains present in the lower without losing its own rank. This idea underlies the author’s language of eternity and coming to be, giving and receiving, descent and ascent.

    ↩

  608. This is the strongest argument for eternity. If a complete, unchanging intellect produces a soul, the soul cannot be material. But if it is immaterial, how can it begin at a particular time? If the soul’s connection or action begins at a particular time while the soul itself is eternal, then it is eternal in its nature—the very claim the argument set out to prove.

    ↩

  609. The argument assumes that whatever is eternal cannot perish, and reverses this to say that whatever does not perish must be eternal. The commentator says each claim needs its own proof; one cannot assume that a true statement stays true when reversed.

    ↩

  610. The earlier argument does not prove that an unlimited number is impossible in every sense. It proves that an unlimited number of things arranged together in an order is impossible. The objection about counting assumes more than that proof establishes.

    ↩

  611. The commentator says the argument does not need the universal claim that everything divisible has continuous unity. It concerns only something that is genuinely one and divides into real parts. Souls are not divided like a kind into its species, or a whole into units; those are only divisions made in thought.

    ↩

  612. This question is not unique to this argument. Distinctions do not have to lead to an endless chain or a circle. They can end in a basic difference that explains itself. In this case, saying souls differ by their nature means they differ in kind, which the argument rejects.

    ↩

  613. If the soul’s powers are material, then a soul with no further intellectual development would lose the features that made it distinct once its body perished. If imagination and estimation survive, however, the soul may still keep distinct mental images even without universal knowledge.

    ↩

  614. The “awareness of oneself” mentioned here may mean a mental awareness of one’s position and limits in the body. The argument assumes souls that have not gained intellectual knowledge.

    ↩

  615. This reply works only if every thing whose part is itself a part must have magnitude. The needed claim is that anything with parts of the same kind is extended.

  616. The objection’s explanation does not match its claim of common knowledge. It also speaks of human souls, though the claim was meant to cover every kind of soul.

  617. The commentator offers a further answer. A feature can be essential to the individual it distinguishes, while accidental to the broader kind it divides. “Rational” distinguishes a human being from other animals, though it is not part of the animal kind. This distinction exists in thought, not as an extra thing in reality. In reality, animal and rational form one living being. Likewise, existence makes individuals distinct before we think about their natures.

    ↩

  618. This is an argument from purpose. Material kinds have many individuals because matter cannot last forever in one individual. The kind is preserved through a succession of individuals. Separate intellects do not need this succession.

    ↩

  619. The soul changes in its substantial existence, yet something remains through the change. The stable part may be the underlying subject, the soul’s relation to God, or the identity formed by existence itself. In a changing being, continued existence may consist in continued change.

    ↩

  620. The image is of fresh water taking on the taste and smell of whatever vessel holds it. Souls receive different features from their bodies, and retain a trace of those differences.

    ↩

  621. Philosophers often call an accidental feature that is not part of a thing’s nature something that happens by chance. This does not mean there is no cause at all; it means the feature does not come from the thing’s nature.
